NotesPractice · 67 questions

Unit 1 · 5–10% of exam

Basic Economic Concepts

1.1

1.1 Scarcity

  • Scarcity exists because wants are unlimited and resources are limited. Every society has to choose how to use its resources, and every choice involves a trade-off.
  • The factors of production are land (natural resources), labor, capital (tools, machines, buildings, and the skills called human capital), and entrepreneurship.
  • In economics, capital means goods used to produce other goods. It does not mean money.
  • Positive statements describe what is and can be tested with data. Normative statements say what ought to be and rest on value judgments.

Watch outScarcity is not the same as a shortage. A shortage happens at a particular price and can end; scarcity is permanent.

Practice 1.1 · 2 questions

1.2

1.2 Opportunity Cost and the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

  • Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
  • The production possibilities curve shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology fully and efficiently used.
  • Points on the curve are efficient. Points inside it are inefficient, as when workers are unemployed in a recession. Points outside it are unattainable with current resources.
  • A curve that is bowed outward shows increasing opportunity cost, because resources are not equally suited to both goods. A straight-line PPC shows constant opportunity cost.
  • The curve shifts outward with more or better resources or improved technology. That shift is economic growth. Producing more capital goods today shifts the curve out faster in the future.
Opportunity cost on a PPC

Watch outA fall in unemployment moves the economy from inside the curve toward the curve. It does not shift the curve.

Practice 1.2 · 4 questions

1.3

1.3 Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

  • A producer has an absolute advantage when it can make more of a good with the same resources, or make a unit with fewer resources.
  • A producer has a comparative advantage when it has the lower opportunity cost of making a good.
  • One producer can have an absolute advantage in both goods, but not a comparative advantage in both.
  • Each side should specialize in the good in which it has a comparative advantage and trade for the other.
  • Trade benefits both sides when the terms of trade fall between the two producers' opportunity costs.
Output problems
Input problems

Watch outCheck whether a table gives outputs (how much can be made) or inputs (hours needed per unit). With input data, the smaller number is the absolute advantage.

Practice 1.3 · 4 questions

1.4

1.4 Demand

  • The law of demand: when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, all else equal. The demand curve slopes downward.
  • A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve, called a change in quantity demanded.
  • A change in demand shifts the whole curve. The shifters are tastes, income, prices of related goods, expectations, and the number of buyers.
  • Normal goods: demand rises when income rises. Inferior goods: demand falls when income rises.
  • Substitutes: a higher price for one raises demand for the other. Complements: a higher price for one lowers demand for the other.

Watch outA change in the good's own price never shifts its demand curve.

Practice 1.4 · 3 questions

1.5

1.5 Supply

  • The law of supply: when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, all else equal. The supply curve slopes upward.
  • A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the supply curve.
  • A change in supply shifts the whole curve. The shifters are input prices, technology, taxes and subsidies, prices of other goods the firm could produce, producer expectations, and the number of sellers.
  • Lower costs or better technology shift supply right. Higher costs or new taxes shift it left.

Practice 1.5 · 2 questions

1.6

1.6 Market Equilibrium, Disequilibrium, and Changes in Equilibrium

  • Equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
  • Above the equilibrium price there is a surplus (quantity supplied is greater), which pushes the price down. Below it there is a shortage (quantity demanded is greater), which pushes the price up.
  • One curve shifts: demand up raises price and quantity; demand down lowers both; supply up lowers price and raises quantity; supply down raises price and lowers quantity.
  • Both curves shift: one of price or quantity is certain and the other is indeterminate without knowing the sizes of the shifts.

ExampleDemand and supply both increase. Each shift raises quantity, so quantity rises. The demand shift raises price and the supply shift lowers it, so the change in price is indeterminate.

Watch outFor a double shift, work out each shift separately, then combine. Where the two effects agree the result is certain; where they conflict it is indeterminate.

Practice 1.6 · 4 questions

Unit 2 · 12–17% of exam

Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle

2.1

2.1 The Circular Flow and GDP

  • The circular flow model links households and firms through two markets. In the product market, households buy goods and services from firms. In the factor market, firms pay households wages, rent, interest, and profit for labor, land, capital, and entrepreneurship.
  • Government, the financial sector, and the foreign sector add leakages (taxes, saving, imports) and injections (government purchases, investment, exports).
  • GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period, usually one year.
  • Three approaches give the same total: expenditures (), income (wages + rent + interest + profit), and value added (the sum of the value added at each stage of production).
  • Investment () is business spending on capital goods, new construction (including new homes), and changes in inventories. Government purchases () exclude transfer payments.
  • Not counted: intermediate goods, used goods, purely financial transactions such as stocks and bonds, transfer payments, unpaid household work, and illegal or unreported activity.
Expenditures approach

Watch outBuying shares of stock is not investment in the GDP sense. Imports are subtracted because they were already counted inside , , or but were not produced domestically.

Practice 2.1 · 3 questions

2.2

2.2 Limitations of GDP

  • GDP measures output, not well-being. It leaves out nonmarket activity (household production, volunteer work), the underground economy, leisure time, and environmental damage.
  • GDP says nothing about how income is distributed or what kinds of goods are produced.
  • GDP can rise because of bad events, such as cleanup spending after a disaster.
  • GDP per capita (GDP divided by population) is a better, though still imperfect, indicator of the standard of living than total GDP.

Watch outWhen paid work is replaced by unpaid work (or the reverse), measured GDP changes even though the amount of production does not.

Practice 2.2 · 2 questions

2.3

2.3 Unemployment

  • The labor force is everyone 16 or older who is employed or unemployed. To count as unemployed, a person must have no job, be available for work, and have actively looked for work in the past four weeks.
  • People not in the labor force include full-time students, retirees, stay-at-home parents, and discouraged workers who have stopped looking.
  • Frictional unemployment: people between jobs or entering the labor force. Structural: skills or locations do not match available jobs, often because of technology or shifts in demand. Cyclical: caused by a recession.
  • The natural rate of unemployment is frictional plus structural unemployment. It is the unemployment rate when the economy produces full-employment output, so cyclical unemployment is zero. It can change slowly over time.
  • The official rate can understate joblessness because it ignores discouraged workers and counts part-time workers who want full-time work as employed.
Labor force
Unemployment rate
Participation rate

Watch outDivide the number of unemployed by the labor force, never by the whole population. Full employment does not mean zero unemployment.

Practice 2.3 · 4 questions

2.4

2.4 Price Indices and Inflation

  • The consumer price index (CPI) compares the cost of a fixed market basket of goods and services with its cost in a base year. The base-year CPI is 100.
  • Inflation is a sustained rise in the overall price level. Deflation is a falling price level. Disinflation is a falling inflation rate while prices still rise.
  • Real values are adjusted for price changes; nominal values are not. Percent change in real income is about the percent change in nominal income minus the inflation rate.
  • The CPI tends to overstate inflation because of substitution bias (the basket is fixed even when consumers switch to cheaper goods), new products, and unmeasured quality improvements.
CPI
Inflation rate
Deflating

Watch outThe inflation rate is a percent change, not the change in index points. Always divide by the earlier CPI.

Practice 2.4 · 5 questions

2.5

2.5 Costs of Inflation

  • Unexpected inflation arbitrarily redistributes wealth. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans gain because they repay with dollars that buy less. Lenders, savers earning fixed interest, people on fixed incomes, and holders of cash lose.
  • Unexpected deflation or disinflation does the reverse: lenders gain and borrowers lose.
  • If inflation is correctly anticipated, lenders build it into nominal interest rates and workers into wage contracts, so little wealth is redistributed.
  • Inflation also erodes the purchasing power of money and creates uncertainty that discourages long-term contracts and investment.
Real interest rate

Practice 2.5 · 2 questions

2.6

2.6 Real v. Nominal GDP

  • Nominal GDP values this year's output at this year's prices. It can rise because of more output, higher prices, or both.
  • Real GDP values this year's output at base-year prices, so it changes only when output changes. Economic growth is measured with real GDP.
  • The GDP deflator is a price index for all goods and services in GDP. In the base year, nominal GDP equals real GDP and the deflator is 100.
  • Percent change in nominal GDP is about the percent change in real GDP plus the inflation rate.
Nominal GDP
Real GDP
GDP deflator

Practice 2.6 · 4 questions

2.7

2.7 Business Cycles

  • The business cycle is the fluctuation of real GDP around its long-run growth trend. Phases: expansion and recession (contraction). Turning points: peak and trough.
  • Potential output, also called full-employment output, is real GDP when unemployment equals the natural rate.
  • The output gap is actual output minus potential output. A negative (recessionary) gap means output is below potential and unemployment is above the natural rate. A positive (inflationary) gap means output is above potential and unemployment is below the natural rate.
  • In a recession, real GDP falls and cyclical unemployment rises. Near a peak, unemployment is low and inflation pressure is high.
Output gap

Practice 2.7 · 2 questions

Unit 3 · 17–27% of exam

National Income and Price Determination

3.1

3.1 Aggregate Demand (AD)

  • Aggregate demand shows the total real GDP demanded by households, firms, government, and the rest of the world at each price level.
  • AD slopes downward for three reasons. Real wealth effect: a lower price level raises the purchasing power of money and assets, so consumption rises. Interest rate effect: a lower price level lowers interest rates, so investment rises. Exchange rate effect: a lower price level makes domestic goods cheaper relative to foreign goods, so net exports rise.
  • A change in the price level causes a movement along AD. A change in , , , or at every price level shifts AD.
  • AD shifts right when consumer or business confidence rises, wealth rises, taxes fall, government purchases rise, interest rates fall for reasons other than the price level, trading partners' incomes rise, or the domestic currency depreciates.

Watch outA change in the price level never shifts AD. It only moves the economy along the curve.

Practice 3.1 · 2 questions

3.2

3.2 Multipliers

  • The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is the fraction of each extra dollar of disposable income that is spent. The marginal propensity to save (MPS) is the fraction saved.
  • An initial change in spending sets off rounds of further spending, so GDP changes by a multiple of the initial change. The expenditure multiplier applies to autonomous changes in , , , or .
  • The tax multiplier is smaller in size because households save part of any tax cut before spending the rest. Its sign is negative: taxes and GDP move in opposite directions. Transfer payments use the same size multiplier with a positive sign.
  • Equal increases in government purchases and taxes raise GDP by the amount of the increase (balanced-budget multiplier of 1).
  • A larger MPC means larger multipliers.
MPC and MPS
Expenditure multiplier
Tax multiplier
Total effect

ExampleWith MPC = 0.9, the expenditure multiplier is and the tax multiplier is . A $10 billion rise in government purchases raises GDP by up to $100 billion; a $10 billion tax cut raises it by up to $90 billion.

Practice 3.2 · 4 questions

3.3

3.3 Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)

  • Short-run aggregate supply shows the total real GDP firms produce at each price level while some input prices are fixed.
  • SRAS slopes upward because nominal wages and other input prices are sticky in the short run. When the price level rises and costs do not, profit per unit rises and firms produce more.
  • Moving along SRAS involves a short-run trade-off: higher output and lower unemployment come with a higher price level.
  • SRAS shifts when production costs change at every price level: input prices (wages, oil, raw materials), productivity, business taxes, subsidies, regulation, and expected inflation. Higher costs shift SRAS left; lower costs shift it right.

Watch outA change in the price level is a movement along SRAS, not a shift.

Practice 3.3 · 2 questions

3.4

3.4 Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS)

  • In the long run all wages and prices are fully flexible, so output returns to full-employment (potential) output whatever the price level. The LRAS curve is vertical at potential output.
  • LRAS matches the production possibilities curve: it shifts right when the economy's productive capacity grows.
  • LRAS shifts with the quantity and quality of resources (labor, physical capital, natural resources), human capital, and technology. A rightward shift is economic growth.
  • Changes in the price level or in aggregate demand do not shift LRAS.

Watch outAnything that raises potential output, such as better technology, shifts both LRAS and SRAS to the right.

Practice 3.4 · 2 questions

3.5

3.5 Equilibrium in the AD–AS Model

  • Short-run equilibrium is where AD crosses SRAS. It sets the price level and real GDP.
  • Long-run equilibrium is where AD, SRAS, and LRAS all cross. Output equals potential and unemployment equals the natural rate.
  • Recessionary (negative output) gap: short-run equilibrium output is below potential, to the left of LRAS. Unemployment is above the natural rate.
  • Inflationary (positive output) gap: short-run equilibrium output is above potential, to the right of LRAS. Unemployment is below the natural rate.

Watch outOn a graph, label the vertical axis "price level" and the horizontal axis "real GDP". Full-employment output is where LRAS meets the horizontal axis.

Practice 3.5 · 3 questions

3.6

3.6 Changes in the AD–AS Model in the Short Run

  • AD shifts right (positive demand shock): price level rises, real GDP rises, unemployment falls. Inflation from this source is demand-pull inflation.
  • AD shifts left (negative demand shock): price level falls, real GDP falls, unemployment rises.
  • SRAS shifts left (negative supply shock): price level rises, real GDP falls, unemployment rises. This is cost-push inflation, also called stagflation.
  • SRAS shifts right (positive supply shock): price level falls, real GDP rises, unemployment falls.

Watch outA demand shock moves the price level and output in the same direction. A supply shock moves them in opposite directions.

Practice 3.6 · 3 questions

3.7

3.7 Long-Run Self-Adjustment

  • With no policy action, flexible wages and prices move the economy back to potential output. The adjustment happens through shifts of SRAS.
  • Recessionary gap: high unemployment pushes nominal wages down over time. Lower costs shift SRAS right until output returns to potential at a lower price level.
  • Inflationary gap: a tight labor market pushes nominal wages up. Higher costs shift SRAS left until output returns to potential at a higher price level.
  • In the long run a shift in AD changes only the price level. Real GDP returns to potential and unemployment returns to the natural rate.
  • A shift of LRAS changes potential output itself and represents long-run growth or decline.

Watch outSelf-adjustment works through wages and SRAS. AD does not shift by itself to close a gap.

Practice 3.7 · 3 questions

3.8

3.8 Fiscal Policy

  • Fiscal policy is the use of government purchases, taxes, and transfer payments to influence aggregate demand.
  • Expansionary policy fights a recessionary gap: raise government purchases, cut taxes, or raise transfers. AD shifts right, so real GDP and the price level rise and unemployment falls. The budget moves toward deficit.
  • Contractionary policy fights an inflationary gap: cut government purchases, raise taxes, or cut transfers. AD shifts left, so real GDP and the price level fall. The budget moves toward surplus.
  • Government purchases affect AD directly. Taxes and transfers work indirectly through disposable income and consumption, so a dollar of spending has a larger effect than a dollar of tax change.
  • Discretionary policy has lags: time to recognize the problem, to pass legislation, and for the change to take effect.
Sizing a spending change
Sizing a tax change

Practice 3.8 · 5 questions

3.9

3.9 Automatic Stabilizers

  • Automatic stabilizers are taxes and transfer programs that change with the business cycle without any new legislation.
  • In a recession, incomes fall, so income tax revenue falls and spending on programs such as unemployment insurance rises. Disposable income and consumption fall by less, which cushions the drop in AD. The deficit grows automatically.
  • In an expansion, tax revenue rises and transfer payments fall, which restrains AD and keeps the economy from overheating.
  • Stabilizers reduce the size of business-cycle swings but do not eliminate them. Unlike discretionary policy, they have no decision lag.

Watch outA stimulus bill passed by Congress is discretionary policy, not an automatic stabilizer.

. Transfer payments are left out and imports are subtracted. Adding the $100 billion of transfers gives the wrong answer of $1,170 billion.

Only the final good counts, so GDP rises by $6. The value added at each stage () gives the same total. Adding every sale ($10) double counts the wheat and flour.

Explanation
Real wage . Multiplying by 1.10 instead of dividing gives $24.20.
15

2.5 Costs of Inflation

Question 15. Inflation turns out to be much higher than anyone expected. Who benefits?

Explanation
The borrower repays with dollars worth less than expected. The bank, the retiree, and the cash holder all receive or hold dollars that have lost purchasing power.
16

2.5 Costs of Inflation

Question 16. A bank makes a one-year loan at a fixed nominal interest rate of 6%, expecting 2% inflation. Actual inflation is 5%. What real interest rate does the bank earn, and who gains from the surprise?

Explanation
Real rate , well below the 4% the bank expected. Unexpected inflation transfers wealth from lenders to borrowers.
17

2.6 Real v. Nominal GDP

Question 17. An economy produces only apples and books. In 2020, the base year, it produced 100 apples at $1 each and 50 books at $10 each. In 2025 it produced 120 apples at $2 each and 60 books at $12 each. What is real GDP in 2025?

Explanation
Real GDP values 2025 quantities at base-year prices: . The $960 figure is nominal GDP for 2025, and $600 is GDP in 2020.
18

2.6 Real v. Nominal GDP

Question 18. Nominal GDP is $960 billion and real GDP is $720 billion. What is the GDP deflator, to the nearest whole number?

Explanation
. Dividing real by nominal gives 75, which is upside down.
19

2.6 Real v. Nominal GDP

Question 19. Nominal GDP grows by 6% while the GDP deflator rises by 2%. Real GDP

Explanation
Percent change in real GDP is about nominal growth minus inflation: .
20

2.6 Real v. Nominal GDP

Question 20. Real GDP is $500 billion and the GDP deflator is 120. What is nominal GDP?

Explanation
Nominal GDP . Dividing by 1.20 gives $417 billion, which goes the wrong way.
21

2.7 Business Cycles

Question 21. Starting from a peak, which sequence lists the phases and turning points of the business cycle in order?

Explanation
After a peak, output falls (recession) until it reaches the trough, then rises (expansion) to the next peak.
22

2.7 Business Cycles

Question 22. An economy's actual real GDP is below its potential output. Which statement must be true?

Explanation
Output below potential is a negative (recessionary) gap. Some workers are cyclically unemployed, so the unemployment rate is above the natural rate.

3.1 Aggregate Demand (AD)

Question 1. Which of the following helps explain why the aggregate demand curve slopes downward?

Explanation
This is the interest rate effect. The other two reasons are the real wealth effect and the exchange rate effect. Switching between goods is a microeconomic idea that does not apply when all prices fall together.
2

3.1 Aggregate Demand (AD)

Question 2. Which of the following shifts the aggregate demand curve to the right?

Explanation
Richer trading partners buy more exports, which raises net exports and shifts AD right. A lower price level is a movement along AD; higher taxes and a stronger currency shift AD left.
3

The expenditure multiplier is , and . The $200 billion answer uses the tax multiplier of 4 by mistake.

3.2 Multipliers

Question 6. When disposable income rises from $400 billion to $500 billion, consumption rises from $350 billion to $430 billion. What is the expenditure multiplier?

Explanation
, so the multiplier is . The value 1.25 is , a common slip.
7

3.3 Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)

Question 7. The short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward because

Explanation
Sticky input prices are the key. If wages adjusted at once, profits would not rise with the price level and firms would have no reason to produce more.
8

3.3 Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)

Question 8. A sharp increase in world oil prices will most likely cause

Explanation
Oil is an input for most production. Higher input costs reduce output at every price level, which is a leftward shift of SRAS (a negative supply shock).
9

3.4 Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS)

Question 9. The long-run aggregate supply curve is vertical because, in the long run,

Explanation
Once all prices and wages adjust, a higher price level no longer raises profits, so output stays at potential. Fixed wages describe the short run.
10

3.4 Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS)

Question 10. Which of the following shifts the long-run aggregate supply curve to the right?

Explanation
More capital raises the economy's productive capacity. The other choices affect aggregate demand or are movements along a curve.
11

3.5 Equilibrium in the AD–AS Model

Question 11. Aggregate demand and short-run aggregate supply intersect at a level of real GDP below full-employment output. The economy has

Explanation
Output below potential is a recessionary gap. Fewer workers are needed, so unemployment is above the natural rate.
12

3.5 Equilibrium in the AD–AS Model

Question 12. When an economy is in long-run equilibrium, the unemployment rate is

Explanation
In long-run equilibrium output equals potential, so cyclical unemployment is zero. Frictional and structural unemployment remain, and together they make up the natural rate.
13

3.5 Equilibrium in the AD–AS Model

Question 13. An economy's unemployment rate is 3% and its natural rate of unemployment is 5%. The economy has

Explanation
Unemployment below the natural rate means the economy is producing more than its full-employment output, which is a positive (inflationary) gap.
14

3.6 Changes in the AD–AS Model in the Short Run

Question 14. Consumer confidence falls sharply. In the short run, what happens to the price level, real GDP, and unemployment?

Explanation
Lower confidence reduces consumption, shifting AD left along SRAS. Both the price level and output fall, and unemployment rises.
15

3.6 Changes in the AD–AS Model in the Short Run

Question 15. Stagflation, a rising price level together with falling real GDP, is caused by

Explanation
Only a leftward shift of SRAS raises the price level while lowering output. A leftward AD shift lowers both.
16

3.6 Changes in the AD–AS Model in the Short Run

Question 16. An economy is at full employment when business investment surges. In the short run the result is

Explanation
Investment is part of AD, so AD shifts right. In the short run output rises above potential and the price level rises. Output returns to potential only in the long run.
17

3.7 Long-Run Self-Adjustment

Question 17. An economy is in a recessionary gap and the government takes no action. How does the economy return to full employment in the long run?

Explanation
High unemployment eventually lowers nominal wages. Lower production costs shift SRAS right, raising output back to potential and lowering the price level.
18

3.7 Long-Run Self-Adjustment

Question 18. An economy starts in long-run equilibrium. Aggregate demand then increases and no policy action is taken. Compared with the original equilibrium, the new long-run equilibrium has

Explanation
The inflationary gap raises nominal wages, which shifts SRAS left until output is back at potential. Only the price level ends up higher.
19

3.7 Long-Run Self-Adjustment

Question 19. An economy in long-run equilibrium is hit by a sharp rise in oil prices, and the government takes no action. In the long run,

Explanation
The supply shock creates a recessionary gap. Over time, falling nominal wages lower production costs, so SRAS shifts back and output returns to potential.
20

3.8 Fiscal Policy

Question 20. An economy has an inflationary gap. Which fiscal policy action is appropriate?

Explanation
An inflationary gap calls for contractionary policy. Higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left. The other choices are expansionary.
21

3.8 Fiscal Policy

Question 21. An economy has a recessionary gap of $200 billion and a marginal propensity to consume of 0.75. What is the minimum increase in government purchases that closes the gap?

Explanation
The expenditure multiplier is , and . A tax cut would have to be larger, , because the tax multiplier is smaller.
22

3.8 Fiscal Policy

Question 22. Compared with a $10 billion increase in government purchases, a $10 billion tax cut shifts aggregate demand to the right by

Explanation
Government purchases enter AD directly and in full. Households spend only the MPC share of a tax cut, so the first round of spending is smaller.
23

3.8 Fiscal Policy

Question 23. Which of the following is a reason discretionary fiscal policy may be poorly timed?

Explanation
These recognition, decision, and implementation lags mean a policy may take effect after the economy has already changed.

3.8 Fiscal Policy

Question 24. An economy has an inflationary gap of $120 billion and a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8. By how much should taxes be raised to close the gap?

Explanation
The tax multiplier has size , and . The $24 billion answer is the needed cut in government purchases, which uses the expenditure multiplier of 5.

3.9 Automatic Stabilizers

Question 25. Which of the following is an automatic stabilizer?

Explanation
Unemployment insurance spending rises with no new law being passed. A stimulus bill is discretionary, lower interest rates are monetary policy, and a balanced-budget rule would force cuts during recessions.

3.9 Automatic Stabilizers

Question 26. During an economic expansion, automatic stabilizers cause

Explanation
As incomes rise, people pay more in taxes and fewer qualify for transfers. Both effects slow the growth of disposable income and restrain AD.

AP Chemistry · Units 1–3

Chemistry notes

NotesPractice · 84 questions

Unit 1 · 7–9% of exam

Atomic Structure and Properties

1.1

1.1 Moles and Molar Mass

  • The mole connects the mass of a sample to the number of particles in it. One mole contains particles, which is Avogadro's number ().
  • Molar mass in g/mol has the same numerical value as the average mass of one atom or molecule in amu.
  • Use dimensional analysis to move between grams, moles, and particles. Use the subscripts in a formula to go from molecules to atoms.
Moles from mass
Particles from moles

Watch outCheck whether a question asks for atoms or molecules. One mole of contains two moles of oxygen atoms.

Practice 1.1 · 2 questions

1.2

1.2 Mass Spectra of Elements

  • The mass spectrum of an element has one peak for each isotope. A peak's position gives the isotope's mass, and its height gives the isotope's relative abundance.
  • Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.
  • Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of the isotope masses. It lies closest to the mass of the most abundant isotope.
Weighted average

Watch outDo not take a simple average of the isotope masses. Convert each percent to a decimal and weight each mass.

Practice 1.2 · 2 questions

1.3

1.3 Elemental Composition of Pure Substances

  • A pure substance has a fixed composition. The law of definite proportions says a compound always contains the same elements in the same ratio by mass.
  • The empirical formula is the lowest whole-number ratio of atoms. The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it.
  • To find an empirical formula: treat percents as grams in a 100 g sample, convert to moles, divide by the smallest number of moles, and scale to whole numbers.
Mass percent
Molecular formula

Watch outConvert masses to moles before taking ratios. A ratio of grams is not a ratio of atoms.

Practice 1.3 · 3 questions

1.4

1.4 Composition of Mixtures

  • A mixture contains two or more substances whose proportions can vary. A pure substance has one fixed composition.
  • Elemental analysis measures the mass percent of each element in a sample. Comparing the result with the percent calculated for the pure compound shows whether the sample is pure.
  • If the measured percent of an element is too low, the impurity contains a smaller percent of that element than the compound does (or none). If it is too high, the impurity contains a larger percent.
Mixture composition

Practice 1.4 · 2 questions

1.5

1.5 Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration

  • An atom has a dense nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. Electrons are held by the attraction between opposite charges.
  • Coulomb's law: the force between two charges grows with the size of the charges and shrinks as the distance between them grows.
  • Electrons fill subshells from lowest energy up (Aufbau principle): , , , , , , , . An subshell holds 2 electrons, holds 6, and holds 10.
  • Core electrons are in inner shells. Valence electrons are in the outermost occupied shell.
  • To write a cation's configuration, remove electrons from the highest shell first. Transition metals lose their electrons before their electrons.
  • Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom or ion in the gas phase.
Coulomb's law

Watch out is . The two electrons are removed, not two electrons.

Practice 1.5 · 3 questions

1.6

1.6 Photoelectron Spectroscopy

  • Photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) measures the energy needed to remove electrons from each subshell of an atom.
  • Each peak is one subshell. The peak's position is the binding energy: electrons closer to the nucleus have higher binding energy, so is always highest.
  • The peak's height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
  • Reading the peak heights in order gives the electron configuration and identifies the element.
  • For the same subshell, an atom with more protons has a higher binding energy.

Watch outHeight tells you how many electrons. Position tells you how strongly they are held. Check which direction the energy axis runs before reading a spectrum.

Practice 1.6 · 3 questions

1.7

1.7 Periodic Trends

  • Trends follow from Coulomb's law: the attraction depends on effective nuclear charge and on the distance of the valence electrons from the nucleus (the number of shells).
  • Atomic radius decreases across a period (more protons pulling on the same shell) and increases down a group (more shells).
  • First ionization energy increases across a period and decreases down a group. Electronegativity follows the same pattern; fluorine is highest.
  • Ionic radius: cations are smaller than their atoms and anions are larger. In an isoelectronic series, the ion with the most protons is the smallest.
  • Successive ionization energies rise steadily, then jump sharply when the first core electron is removed. The number of electrons removed before the jump is the number of valence electrons.
  • Electron affinity generally becomes more negative across a period.

Watch outExplain a trend with protons, shells, and attraction. Saying an atom "wants a full octet" or naming the trend is not an explanation.

Practice 1.7 · 5 questions

1.8

1.8 Valence Electrons and Ionic Compounds

  • Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they react in similar ways and form compounds with similar formulas, such as and .
  • Typical ion charges: group 1 forms 1+, group 2 forms 2+, group 13 forms 3+, group 15 forms 3−, group 16 forms 2−, group 17 forms 1−.
  • The formula of an ionic compound is the smallest whole-number ratio of ions that gives a total charge of zero.

Example and need a total of 6+ and 6−, so the formula is .

Practice 1.8 · 2 questions

Unit 2 · 7–9% of exam

Compound Structure and Properties

2.1

2.1 Types of Chemical Bonds

  • Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract shared electrons. The difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms sets the bond type.
  • Nonpolar covalent: electrons shared equally (identical atoms or very similar electronegativity). Polar covalent: electrons shared unequally, giving partial charges. Ionic: electrons transferred, usually between a metal and a nonmetal. Metallic: valence electrons delocalized among metal atoms.
  • The greater the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond. The more electronegative atom carries the partial negative charge.
  • Bonding is a continuum. The properties of a substance, such as conductivity when melted, are the best evidence for its bond type.

Practice 2.1 · 3 questions

2.2

2.2 Intramolecular Force and Potential Energy

  • A graph of potential energy versus the distance between two nuclei has a minimum. The distance at the minimum is the bond length, and the depth of the minimum is the bond energy, the energy needed to break the bond.
  • At shorter distances, repulsion raises the potential energy sharply. At large distances the atoms do not interact and the potential energy approaches zero.
  • Higher bond order means a shorter and stronger bond: triple < double < single in length.
  • For ions, Coulomb's law applies: attraction is stronger when the charges are larger and the ions are smaller (closer together).

Watch outA stronger bond sits lower on the potential energy graph (a deeper well), not higher.

Practice 2.2 · 4 questions

2.3

2.3 Structure of Ionic Solids

  • An ionic solid is a three-dimensional lattice of alternating cations and anions. The arrangement maximizes attraction between opposite charges and minimizes repulsion between like charges.
  • Ionic solids have high melting points and are hard but brittle.
  • They do not conduct electricity as solids because the ions are fixed in place. They conduct when melted or dissolved because the ions can move.
  • There are no separate molecules. The formula gives the ratio of ions.

Practice 2.3 · 2 questions

2.4

2.4 Structure of Metals and Alloys

  • In a metal, positive metal ions sit in a lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalized valence electrons.
  • Mobile electrons explain electrical and thermal conductivity. Because the bonding is not directional, layers can slide without breaking the solid, so metals are malleable and ductile.
  • Interstitial alloy: small atoms fill the spaces between larger metal atoms, as carbon does in steel. The result is usually harder and less malleable.
  • Substitutional alloy: atoms of similar size replace some of the metal atoms, as zinc does in brass.

Watch outUse atomic radius to decide the alloy type: much smaller atoms give an interstitial alloy; similar-sized atoms give a substitutional alloy.

Practice 2.4 · 2 questions

2.5

2.5 Lewis Diagrams

  • Count the total valence electrons, adding one for each negative charge and subtracting one for each positive charge.
  • Join the atoms with single bonds (least electronegative atom in the center, never hydrogen), complete the octets of the outer atoms, and place any remaining electrons on the central atom.
  • If the central atom lacks an octet, turn lone pairs on outer atoms into double or triple bonds.
  • Exceptions to the octet rule: hydrogen holds 2 electrons; boron and beryllium may have fewer than 8; elements in period 3 and below may hold more than 8.

Practice 2.5 · 2 questions

2.6

2.6 Resonance and Formal Charge

  • Resonance occurs when two or more valid Lewis diagrams differ only in where the electrons are placed. The real molecule is an average of them, called a resonance hybrid.
  • In a resonance hybrid the electrons are delocalized, and the bonds involved are identical, with lengths and strengths between those of single and double bonds.
  • Formal charge helps choose the best diagram. Prefer formal charges closest to zero, with any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom. Formal charges add up to the overall charge.
Formal charge

Watch outA molecule does not flip back and forth between resonance structures. It has one structure, the hybrid.

Practice 2.6 · 3 questions

2.7

2.7 VSEPR and Hybridization

  • VSEPR: electron domains around a central atom spread as far apart as possible. A domain is a lone pair or a bond; a double or triple bond counts as one domain.
  • 2 domains: linear, 180°, . 3 domains: trigonal planar, 120°, ; with one lone pair the shape is bent. 4 domains: tetrahedral, 109.5°, ; one lone pair gives trigonal pyramidal (about 107°); two give bent (about 104.5°).
  • 5 domains: trigonal bipyramidal (90° and 120°); lone pairs give seesaw, T-shaped, then linear. 6 domains: octahedral (90°); lone pairs give square pyramidal, then square planar.
  • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so they squeeze the bond angles.
  • A single bond is one sigma (σ) bond. A double bond is one σ and one pi (π) bond. A triple bond is one σ and two π bonds.
  • A molecule is polar when its bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetric shapes with identical outer atoms, such as , , and , are nonpolar.

Watch outCount domains on the central atom from the Lewis diagram first. Name the molecular shape from the positions of the atoms only, not the lone pairs.

Practice 2.7 · 7 questions

Unit 3 · 18–22% of exam

Properties of Substances and Mixtures

3.1

3.1 Intermolecular and Interparticle Forces

  • London dispersion forces act between all particles. They come from temporary dipoles and grow stronger with more electrons (a more polarizable electron cloud) and with more surface contact between molecules.
  • Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules.
  • Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole–dipole attraction: a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O, or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O, or F in another molecule.
  • Ion–dipole forces act between ions and polar molecules, as when a salt dissolves in water.
  • Stronger intermolecular forces mean a higher boiling point, higher melting point, and lower vapor pressure.

Watch outBoiling a molecular substance separates molecules from each other. It does not break the covalent bonds inside the molecules.

Practice 3.1 · 5 questions

3.2

3.2 Properties of Solids

  • Ionic solids: ions held by strong electrostatic attraction. High melting point, brittle, conduct only when melted or dissolved.
  • Molecular solids: separate molecules held by intermolecular forces. Low melting point, soft, do not conduct. Examples: ice, , dry ice, sugar.
  • Covalent network solids: atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout the whole solid. Very high melting point and very hard. Examples: diamond, , .
  • Metallic solids: metal ions in a sea of electrons. Conduct as solids and are malleable.
  • Graphite is a network solid made of sheets. Each carbon bonds to three others, and the leftover electrons are delocalized, so graphite conducts and its sheets slide.
  • Crystalline solids have an ordered, repeating arrangement. Amorphous solids do not.

Practice 3.2 · 3 questions

3.3

3.3 Solids, Liquids, and Gases

  • Solid: particles packed closely in fixed positions; they only vibrate. Fixed shape and volume.
  • Liquid: particles close together but able to move past one another. Fixed volume, takes the shape of its container.
  • Gas: particles far apart, moving constantly and randomly, with negligible attractions. Fills its container and is easily compressed.
  • The solid and liquid phases of a substance have similar molar volumes because the particles are in close contact in both.
  • The phase depends on the balance between intermolecular forces and the kinetic energy of the particles.

Practice 3.3 · 2 questions

3.4

3.4 Ideal Gas Law

  • The ideal gas law relates pressure, volume, moles, and temperature. Temperature must be in kelvin.
  • With moles fixed, use the combined gas law. Pressure and volume are inversely related; volume and pressure are each directly related to kelvin temperature.
  • Dalton's law: the total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures. Each partial pressure equals the gas's mole fraction times the total pressure.
  • At STP (273 K and 1 atm), one mole of an ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L.
Ideal gas law
Combined gas law
Dalton's law
Molar mass from density

Watch outConvert Celsius to kelvin before using any gas law: .

Practice 3.4 · 6 questions

3.5

3.5 Kinetic Molecular Theory

  • Gas particles are in constant, random motion. An ideal gas has particles of negligible volume, with no attractions between them and perfectly elastic collisions.
  • Pressure comes from collisions of particles with the container walls.
  • The average kinetic energy of gas particles depends only on the kelvin temperature. All gases at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy.
  • At the same temperature, lighter particles move faster on average.
  • A Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows the spread of particle speeds. Raising the temperature makes the curve broader and flatter and moves its peak to higher speed.
Kinetic energy

Practice 3.5 · 2 questions

3.6

3.6 Deviation from Ideal Gas Law

  • Real gases deviate from ideal behavior most at low temperature and high pressure, when particles are slow and close together.
  • Attractive forces between particles make the measured pressure lower than the ideal prediction, because particles strike the walls with less force.
  • Particle volume matters at very high pressure. The particles take up part of the container, so the measured pressure is higher than the ideal prediction.
  • Gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure. Small particles with weak attractions, such as He, come closest to ideal.

Practice 3.6 · 3 questions

3.7

3.7 Solutions and Mixtures

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture: its composition is uniform throughout at the particle level. A heterogeneous mixture has regions with different compositions.
  • Solutions can be solids (alloys), liquids, or gases (air).
  • Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution.
  • Diluting a solution adds solvent but leaves the moles of solute unchanged.
Molarity
Dilution

Watch outMolarity uses liters of solution, not liters of solvent. Convert mL to L.

Practice 3.7 · 3 questions

3.8

3.8 Representations of Solutions

  • A particulate drawing of a solution should show the correct relative numbers of solute particles and how the solute and solvent particles interact.
  • Soluble ionic compounds separate into individual ions in water, in the ratio given by the formula. Molecular solutes such as sugar stay as whole molecules.
  • Water molecules orient around ions: the oxygen end (partial negative) points toward cations, and the hydrogen ends (partial positive) point toward anions. These are ion–dipole attractions.

Watch outDo not draw dissolved ionic compounds as molecules. (aq) is one ion and two separate ions, not .

Practice 3.8 · 2 questions

3.9

3.9 Separation of Solutions and Mixtures

  • Separation methods use differences in intermolecular forces and physical properties.
  • Filtration separates an undissolved solid from a liquid. It cannot remove a dissolved solute.
  • Evaporation recovers a dissolved solid by removing the solvent.
  • Distillation separates liquids with different boiling points. The component with weaker intermolecular forces vaporizes first.
  • Chromatography separates components that are attracted differently to a mobile phase (the moving solvent) and a stationary phase (such as paper). A component attracted more to the mobile phase travels farther.

Practice 3.9 · 2 questions

3.10

3.10 Solubility

  • Substances with similar intermolecular forces tend to dissolve in each other: "like dissolves like."
  • Ionic and polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents such as water. Nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents such as hexane.
  • A solute dissolves when solute–solvent attractions are about as strong as the solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions they replace.
  • Molecules that can hydrogen-bond with water, such as small alcohols, are very soluble. A longer nonpolar carbon chain lowers solubility in water.

Practice 3.10 · 2 questions

3.11

3.11 Spectroscopy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum

  • Different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum cause different changes in molecules and atoms.
  • Microwave radiation changes how molecules rotate.
  • Infrared radiation changes how bonds vibrate. It is used to identify the types of bonds in a molecule.
  • Ultraviolet and visible radiation move electrons between energy levels.
  • From lowest to highest photon energy: microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet.

Practice 3.11 · 2 questions

3.12

3.12 Properties of Photons

  • Light has wave properties: wavelength () and frequency () are inversely related through the speed of light.
  • Light also comes in packets of energy called photons. Higher frequency, or shorter wavelength, means more energy per photon.
  • An atom or molecule absorbs or emits a photon only when the photon's energy equals the difference between two of its energy levels.
Wave equation
Photon energy

Watch outConvert nanometers to meters before calculating: .

Practice 3.12 · 4 questions

3.13

3.13 Beer–Lambert Law

  • Absorbance is proportional to concentration. is the molar absorptivity (how strongly the substance absorbs at that wavelength), is the path length, and is the concentration.
  • With the same substance, cuvette, and wavelength, absorbance and concentration are directly proportional. A graph of absorbance versus concentration for known solutions (a calibration curve) is a straight line used to find an unknown concentration.
  • Measure at the wavelength where the substance absorbs most strongly.
  • Common errors: a smudged cuvette scatters light and raises the absorbance reading; water left in the cuvette dilutes the sample and lowers it.
Beer–Lambert law

Practice 3.13 · 3 questions

One formula unit contains two nitrogen atoms: . Counting only one nitrogen gives 17.5%.

AP Biology · Units 1–3

Biology notes

NotesPractice · 60 questions

Unit 1 · 8–11% of exam

Chemistry of Life

1.1

1.1 Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding

  • Water is a polar molecule. Oxygen pulls shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, so the oxygen end is partially negative and the hydrogen ends are partially positive.
  • A hydrogen bond is the attraction between a partially positive hydrogen on one molecule and a partially negative atom (oxygen or nitrogen) on another. Each one is weak, but together they are strong.
  • Cohesion: water molecules stick to each other. It produces surface tension.
  • Adhesion: water molecules stick to other polar or charged surfaces. Cohesion and adhesion together move water up plant xylem (capillary action).
  • Hydrogen bonding also gives water a high specific heat (it resists temperature change), a high heat of vaporization (evaporative cooling), ice that is less dense than liquid water, and the ability to dissolve polar and ionic substances.

Watch outHydrogen bonds form between water molecules. The bonds inside one water molecule are polar covalent bonds.

Practice 1.1 · 3 questions

1.2

1.2 Elements of Life

  • Living systems exchange matter with the environment to grow, reproduce, and stay organized.
  • Carbon forms the backbone of all four classes of macromolecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
  • Nitrogen is needed to build proteins and nucleic acids.
  • Phosphorus is needed to build nucleic acids and certain lipids, such as phospholipids.
  • Sulfur is found in some amino acids, so it is used to build proteins.
  • Carbohydrates and most lipids contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.

Practice 1.2 · 2 questions

1.3

1.3 Introduction to Macromolecules

  • Most macromolecules are polymers built from smaller units called monomers.
  • Dehydration synthesis joins monomers with a covalent bond and releases one molecule of water for each bond formed.
  • Hydrolysis breaks a polymer apart by adding water across the bond. Digestion works by hydrolysis.
  • Monomers and their polymers: monosaccharides form polysaccharides, amino acids form proteins, and nucleotides form nucleic acids. Lipids are not true polymers.

Watch outDehydration synthesis releases water and builds. Hydrolysis uses water and breaks.

Practice 1.3 · 2 questions

1.4

1.4 Carbohydrates

  • Carbohydrates are made of sugar monomers (monosaccharides, such as glucose) joined by covalent glycosidic bonds into polysaccharides.
  • Carbohydrate polymers can be linear or branched.
  • Storage polysaccharides: starch in plants and glycogen in animals. Glycogen is highly branched.
  • Structural polysaccharides: cellulose in plant cell walls and chitin in fungal cell walls and arthropod exoskeletons.
  • Starch and cellulose are both made of glucose. They differ in how the glucose units are linked, which gives them different shapes and functions.

Practice 1.4 · 2 questions

1.5

1.5 Lipids

  • Lipids are nonpolar and hydrophobic. They include fats, phospholipids, and steroids.
  • A fat is glycerol joined to three fatty acids. Fats store energy.
  • Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds, are straight, pack tightly, and are usually solid at room temperature.
  • Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds that put kinks in the chain. They pack loosely and are usually liquid at room temperature.
  • A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails. In water, phospholipids form a bilayer.
  • Steroids, such as cholesterol, have four fused carbon rings.

Practice 1.5 · 2 questions

1.6

1.6 Nucleic Acids

  • Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.
  • DNA: the sugar is deoxyribose; the bases are A, T, G, and C; it is usually a double helix of two antiparallel strands.
  • RNA: the sugar is ribose; uracil (U) replaces thymine; it is usually single-stranded.
  • Each strand has directionality: a 5′ end with a free phosphate and a 3′ end with a free hydroxyl. New nucleotides are added only to the 3′ end.
  • Nucleotides in a strand are joined by covalent bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone. The two DNA strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases: A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G pairs with C (three hydrogen bonds).

Watch outCovalent bonds hold each strand together. Hydrogen bonds hold the two strands to each other.

Practice 1.6 · 3 questions

1.7

1.7 Proteins

  • Proteins are polymers of amino acids. Each amino acid has a central carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and an R group.
  • R groups can be hydrophobic (nonpolar), hydrophilic (polar), or charged. Their properties determine how the protein folds.
  • Amino acids are joined by covalent peptide bonds between the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the next. A polypeptide has an amino end (N-terminus) and a carboxyl end (C-terminus).
  • Primary structure: the sequence of amino acids. Secondary: alpha helices and beta sheets formed by hydrogen bonds in the backbone. Tertiary: the overall three-dimensional shape, formed by interactions among R groups. Quaternary: two or more polypeptides joined together.
  • A protein's shape determines its function. Denaturation (by heat or pH change) disrupts shape and function without breaking peptide bonds.

Watch outSecondary structure comes from the backbone. Tertiary structure comes from the R groups.

Practice 1.7 · 3 questions

Unit 2 · 10–13% of exam

Cells

2.1

2.1 Cell Structure and Function

  • Ribosomes build proteins from the instructions in mRNA. They are made of rRNA and protein and are found in all cells, which is evidence of common ancestry.
  • Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes attached and makes proteins for membranes and for export. Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies.
  • The Golgi complex is a stack of membrane sacs that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins into vesicles.
  • Mitochondria have a double membrane. The folded inner membrane (cristae) provides a large surface for ATP production.
  • Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that digest macromolecules and worn-out cell parts.
  • Vacuoles store materials. The large central vacuole of a plant cell holds water and maintains turgor pressure.
  • Chloroplasts have a double membrane, stacks of thylakoids (grana) where the light reactions occur, and a fluid stroma where the Calvin cycle occurs.

Watch outThe path of a secreted protein is ribosome on the rough ER, then Golgi, then vesicle, then plasma membrane.

Practice 2.1 · 3 questions

2.2

2.2 Cell Size

  • Cells exchange materials and heat with their surroundings across their surface, but their needs depend on their volume.
  • As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so its surface area-to-volume ratio falls.
  • A higher ratio means more efficient exchange. This limits how large a cell can be.
  • Folds and extensions such as microvilli and root hairs increase surface area without adding much volume.
  • The same idea applies to whole organisms: a smaller animal has a higher ratio, loses heat faster, and has a higher metabolic rate per unit of body mass.
Cube
Sphere

Practice 2.2 · 3 questions

2.3

2.3 Plasma Membrane

  • The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer. Hydrophilic heads face the watery inside and outside of the cell; hydrophobic tails face each other.
  • Embedded proteins have hydrophobic regions inside the bilayer and hydrophilic regions exposed to water.
  • The fluid mosaic model: the membrane is a moving mixture of phospholipids, proteins, cholesterol, glycoproteins, and glycolipids.
  • Cholesterol helps regulate membrane fluidity. Glycoproteins and glycolipids act in cell recognition.

Practice 2.3 · 2 questions

2.4

2.4 Membrane Permeability

  • The hydrophobic interior of the bilayer makes the membrane selectively permeable.
  • Small nonpolar molecules, such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen, pass freely through the bilayer.
  • Ions and large polar molecules cannot pass through the bilayer and need channel or transport proteins.
  • Small polar molecules such as water pass through the bilayer only in small amounts. Most water crosses through channel proteins called aquaporins.
  • Cell walls of plants (cellulose), fungi (chitin), and prokaryotes give structure and are an additional barrier outside the membrane.

Practice 2.4 · 2 questions

2.5

2.5 Membrane Transport

  • Passive transport is the net movement of a substance from higher to lower concentration. It needs no energy from the cell.
  • Active transport moves a substance from lower to higher concentration. It needs energy, usually from ATP, and a transport protein.
  • Endocytosis takes large materials into the cell in vesicles formed from the plasma membrane. Exocytosis releases materials when vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane. Both need energy.
  • Selective transport lets a cell build and keep concentration gradients.

Practice 2.5 · 2 questions

2.6

2.6 Facilitated Diffusion

  • Facilitated diffusion is passive transport through a membrane protein. The substance still moves down its concentration gradient, and no energy is used.
  • Channel proteins form pores for specific ions or for water (aquaporins). Carrier proteins change shape to move a specific molecule across.
  • Movement of ions through channels can make a membrane polarized, with different charges on its two sides.
  • Because the number of transport proteins is limited, the rate of facilitated diffusion levels off when all of them are in use.

Watch outFacilitated diffusion uses a protein but not energy. Active transport uses both.

Practice 2.6 · 2 questions

2.7

2.7 Tonicity and Osmoregulation

  • Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane. Water moves from a hypotonic solution (lower solute concentration) to a hypertonic solution (higher solute concentration).
  • In an isotonic solution there is no net movement of water.
  • Animal cells swell and may burst in a hypotonic solution and shrink in a hypertonic one. Plant cells become turgid in a hypotonic solution, which is their healthy state, and undergo plasmolysis in a hypertonic one.
  • Water potential () predicts the direction of water movement. Water moves from higher water potential to lower water potential.
  • Adding solute lowers the solute potential and so lowers water potential. Pressure raises it. In an open container the pressure potential is zero.
  • Osmoregulation keeps water balance. For example, a contractile vacuole pumps excess water out of a freshwater protist.
Water potential
Solute potential

Watch outIn , is in kelvin and is the number of particles each solute unit forms: 1 for sucrose, 2 for NaCl.

Practice 2.7 · 4 questions

2.8

2.8 Mechanisms of Transport

  • Cells use many processes to move ions and molecules: simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport, endocytosis, and exocytosis.
  • A pump uses ATP to move ions against their gradients. The sodium–potassium pump moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions in for each ATP, which helps maintain the membrane potential.
  • Pumps create an electrochemical gradient, a combination of a concentration difference and a charge difference across the membrane.
  • Cotransport (secondary active transport) uses the energy stored in one substance's gradient to move a different substance against its own gradient.

Practice 2.8 · 2 questions

2.9

2.9 Cell Compartmentalization

  • Internal membranes divide a eukaryotic cell into compartments, so that different reactions can occur in different places under different conditions.
  • Compartments keep processes that would interfere with each other apart. For example, the digestive enzymes of a lysosome are kept away from the rest of the cell.
  • Internal membranes also provide extra surface area where reactions occur, as in the inner mitochondrial membrane and the thylakoid membranes.
  • Prokaryotes generally lack membrane-bound organelles, but they have internal regions with specialized functions, such as the nucleoid.

Practice 2.9 · 2 questions

2.10

2.10 Origins of Cell Compartmentalization

  • Membrane-bound organelles are thought to have evolved from once free-living prokaryotes through endosymbiosis: an ancestral cell took in a prokaryote, and the two became dependent on each other.
  • Mitochondria descend from aerobic bacteria. Chloroplasts descend from photosynthetic bacteria.
  • Evidence: both organelles have a double membrane, their own circular DNA, their own ribosomes that resemble those of bacteria, and they reproduce by dividing on their own, as bacteria do.
  • Prokaryotes and eukaryotes share a plasma membrane, ribosomes, and DNA, which points to a common ancestor.

Practice 2.10 · 2 questions

Unit 3 · 12–16% of exam

Cellular Energetics

3.1

3.1 Enzymes

  • Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins. They speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy.
  • The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site. The two must be compatible in shape and charge.
  • Enzymes are not used up. After the products are released, the enzyme can act again.
  • An enzyme does not change the overall energy difference between reactants and products. It only makes the reaction happen faster.

Watch outAn enzyme lowers activation energy. It does not add energy to the reaction or change the free energy of the products.

Practice 3.1 · 2 questions

3.2

3.2 Environmental Impacts on Enzyme Function

  • A change in an enzyme's shape changes its function. Denaturation is a loss of shape caused by temperature or pH outside the enzyme's working range. It is sometimes reversible.
  • Temperature: warming speeds molecules up and causes more collisions between enzyme and substrate, so the rate rises up to an optimum. Above the optimum the enzyme denatures and the rate falls sharply.
  • pH: each enzyme has an optimum. Changing the hydrogen ion concentration disrupts the hydrogen bonds and charges that hold the enzyme's shape.
  • Substrate concentration: the rate rises as substrate is added until all active sites are occupied, then levels off.
  • Competitive inhibitors bind at the active site and block the substrate. Adding more substrate can overcome them.
  • Noncompetitive inhibitors bind at another site (an allosteric site) and change the enzyme's shape. Adding more substrate does not overcome them.

Practice 3.2 · 4 questions

3.3

3.3 Cellular Energy

  • All living systems need a constant input of energy. Energy is never created or destroyed, and every transfer increases disorder, so cells must keep taking in energy to stay organized.
  • Cells couple reactions: an energy-releasing process, such as the breakdown of ATP, is paired with an energy-requiring process to drive it.
  • ATP stores energy in its phosphate bonds. Removing a phosphate (ATP to ADP) releases energy that the cell can use.
  • Energy transfers happen in sequential steps in metabolic pathways, which allows controlled and efficient transfer.
  • Core pathways such as glycolysis are shared by nearly all organisms, which is evidence of common ancestry.

Practice 3.3 · 2 questions

3.4

3.4 Photosynthesis

  • Photosynthesis captures light energy and stores it in sugars. It first evolved in prokaryotes and is the source of the oxygen in the atmosphere.
  • The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes. Chlorophyll in photosystems II and I absorbs light, which excites electrons.
  • Water is split at photosystem II. This replaces the lost electrons and releases oxygen.
  • Electrons pass along an electron transport chain between the photosystems. The energy released pumps hydrogen ions into the thylakoid, forming a proton gradient.
  • Hydrogen ions flow back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. At the end of the chain, electrons reduce NADP+ to NADPH.
  • The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma. It uses ATP and NADPH to build carbohydrates from carbon dioxide.
Overall equation

Watch outThe oxygen released comes from water, not from carbon dioxide. The carbon in sugar comes from carbon dioxide.

Practice 3.4 · 5 questions

3.5

3.5 Cellular Respiration

  • Cellular respiration releases the energy in glucose and stores it in ATP.
  • Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and needs no oxygen. It splits glucose into two pyruvate and yields a net of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
  • Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is oxidized, releasing carbon dioxide. The Krebs cycle, in the mitochondrial matrix, releases more carbon dioxide and produces ATP, NADH, and FADH2.
  • NADH and FADH2 deliver electrons to the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The energy released pumps hydrogen ions into the intermembrane space.
  • Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water.
  • Hydrogen ions flow back through ATP synthase, producing most of the cell's ATP. This is oxidative phosphorylation by chemiosmosis.
  • Fermentation occurs without oxygen. It regenerates NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue, and it produces lactic acid or alcohol and carbon dioxide.
  • When electron transport is uncoupled from ATP production, the energy is released as heat.
Overall equation

Watch outFermentation makes no ATP beyond glycolysis. Its job is to recycle NADH back to NAD+.

Unit 1 · 17 questions

Chemistry of Life

Not started

1

1.1 Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding

Question 1. Water moves upward through the narrow xylem vessels of a tall tree. Which properties of water are most directly responsible?

Explanation
Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules to each other (cohesion) and to the polar walls of the xylem (adhesion), so the water column is pulled upward without breaking.
2

1.1 Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding

Question 2. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules form because

Explanation
Water's polar covalent bonds leave partial charges on each molecule. Opposite partial charges on neighboring molecules attract.
3

1.1 Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding

Question 3. A large lake changes temperature much more slowly than the surrounding land. This is best explained by water's

Explanation
Much of the heat water absorbs goes into disrupting hydrogen bonds instead of speeding up the molecules, so its temperature changes slowly.
4

1.2 Elements of Life

Question 4. A plant is grown in soil that lacks phosphorus. Which molecules will the plant be least able to make?

Explanation
Phosphorus is part of the phosphate groups in nucleotides and in phospholipids. Carbohydrates, fats, and most proteins contain no phosphorus.
5

1.2 Elements of Life

Question 5. Radioactive nitrogen is supplied to growing cells. In which two types of macromolecules will the label appear?

Explanation
Amino acids contain an amino group, and nucleotides contain nitrogenous bases. Carbohydrates and lipids do not contain nitrogen.
6

1.3 Introduction to Macromolecules

Question 6. Ten glucose molecules are joined into a single chain by dehydration synthesis. How many water molecules are released?

Explanation
Each bond formed releases one water molecule, and joining 10 monomers in a chain takes 9 bonds.
7

1.3 Introduction to Macromolecules

Question 7. Which process breaks a protein into amino acids during digestion?

Explanation
Hydrolysis adds a water molecule across each peptide bond and splits the polymer into monomers.
8

1.4 Carbohydrates

Question 8. Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, yet humans can digest starch and not cellulose. The best explanation is that

Explanation
The orientation of the glycosidic bonds differs between the two polymers. Enzymes are specific to the shape of their substrate, so the enzyme that hydrolyzes starch does not fit cellulose.
9

1.4 Carbohydrates

Question 9. Which carbohydrate serves as the main energy-storage molecule in animal cells?

Explanation
Animals store glucose as glycogen, mostly in liver and muscle cells. Starch is the storage form in plants, and cellulose and chitin are structural.
10

1.5 Lipids

Question 10. Olive oil is liquid at room temperature and butter is solid. The best explanation is that the fatty acids in olive oil

Explanation
Unsaturated fatty acids have carbon–carbon double bonds. The kinks keep the molecules apart, which lowers the melting point.
11

1.5 Lipids

Question 11. When phospholipids are placed in water, they form a bilayer because

Explanation
Phospholipids are amphipathic. The arrangement that keeps the nonpolar tails away from water and the polar heads in contact with it is a bilayer.
12

1.6 Nucleic Acids

Question 12. A double-stranded DNA molecule is 30% adenine. What percent of its bases are guanine?

Explanation
Adenine pairs with thymine, so thymine is also 30%. The remaining 40% is split equally between guanine and cytosine: 20% each.
13

1.6 Nucleic Acids

Question 13. Which feature is found in RNA but not in DNA?

Explanation
RNA nucleotides contain ribose and DNA nucleotides contain deoxyribose. RNA also uses uracil in place of thymine.
14

1.6 Nucleic Acids

Question 14. One strand of DNA has the sequence 5′-ATGC-3′. What is the sequence of the complementary strand, written 5′ to 3′?

Explanation
The strands are antiparallel. Pairing gives 3′-TACG-5′, which reads 5′-GCAT-3′ when written in the standard direction.
15

1.7 Proteins

Question 15. A mutation replaces a hydrophilic amino acid on the surface of a protein with a hydrophobic one. Which level of structure is changed first?

Explanation
A change in the amino acid sequence is a change in primary structure. Any changes in folding at higher levels follow from it.
16

1.7 Proteins

Question 16. The tertiary structure of a protein is held in place mainly by

Explanation
Hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and disulfide bridges among R groups fold the chain into its overall shape. Backbone hydrogen bonds form secondary structure.
17

1.7 Proteins

Question 17. An enzyme is heated until it loses its function, yet its amino acid sequence is unchanged. The heat most directly disrupted

Explanation
Denaturation breaks the weak interactions of secondary and tertiary structure. Peptide bonds stay intact, so the sequence does not change.

Explanation

Question 8. An organism that stops taking in energy will eventually die because

Explanation

Explanation

Question 11. A chemical makes the thylakoid membrane leaky to hydrogen ions. The most direct effect on the chloroplast is that
