AP United States History 1 · Units 1–5

APUSH 1 notes

NotesPractice · 185 questions

Unit 1 · 4–6% of exam

Period 1: 1491–1607

1.1

1.1 Contextualizing Period 1

  • In 1491 the Americas were home to millions of people living in diverse, complex societies shaped by their environments. They had no contact with Europe or Africa.
  • Changes in Europe set up exploration: stronger centralized monarchies (Spain completed its unification in 1492), demand for Asian trade goods and a sea route to reach them, the Renaissance and new maritime technology, and religious rivalry sharpened by the Protestant Reformation (1517).
  • Portugal's voyages along the West African coast opened new trade, including a trade in enslaved people.
  • Columbus's voyage in 1492 began lasting contact among Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans. The period ends in 1607 with Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement.
  • Dates to anchor the period: 1492 Columbus's first voyage; 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas; 1517 Protestant Reformation begins; 1521 fall of the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan; 1565 St. Augustine founded; 1588 England defeats the Spanish Armada; 1607 Jamestown.
  • The defeat of the Spanish Armada weakened Spain's control of the Atlantic and opened the way for English colonization.
  • Before contact, Native societies were linked by long-distance trade networks and spoke hundreds of different languages.

Watch outContextualization means describing the broader setting of a development: what was already happening, and why it matters for what came next.

Practice 1.1 · 4 questions

1.2

1.2 Native American Societies Before European Contact

  • Native peoples adapted to and transformed their environments, which produced very different societies in different regions.
  • Maize cultivation spread north from present-day Mexico. In the Southwest it supported settled communities, irrigation, and social diversification (Pueblo peoples).
  • In the Great Basin and on the western Great Plains, dry land and scarce resources led to largely mobile lifestyles based on hunting and gathering.
  • In the Northeast, the Mississippi River Valley, and along the Atlantic seaboard, societies mixed farming with hunting and gathering and built permanent villages. Examples: the Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) and the Mississippian city of Cahokia.
  • In the Northwest and present-day California, peoples lived by hunting, gathering, and fishing; rich ocean resources supported settled communities such as those of the Chinook.
  • Southwest: Ancestral Puebloans built multistory adobe and cliff dwellings, as at Mesa Verde and Chaco Canyon, and the Hohokam dug irrigation canals.
  • Mississippi Valley: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was a city of large earthen mounds with a population in the thousands, supported by maize farming and trade.
  • Northeast: the Iroquois Confederacy joined five nations, lived in longhouses, traced family lines through mothers, and grew the "Three Sisters" of maize, beans, and squash.
  • Great Plains: before horses arrived with the Spanish, Plains peoples hunted bison on foot, and many also farmed along rivers.
  • Pacific coast: the Chinook built cedar plank houses and relied on salmon. The Chumash of California lived in permanent villages and gathered acorns.

Watch outTie each region to its environment. The exam asks how geography shaped a society's economy and settlement pattern.

Practice 1.2 · 6 questions

1.3

1.3 European Exploration in the Americas

  • European states explored for wealth, power, and religion: new sources of gold and trade, an edge over rival kingdoms, and converts to Christianity.
  • Portugal led early, sailing around Africa to reach Asia. Spain backed Columbus's westward voyage in 1492.
  • The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal.
  • New technology made long voyages possible: the caravel, the compass, the astrolabe, and better maps.
  • France and England began exploring later, looking for a northwest passage to Asia.
  • Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored Portuguese voyages. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498.
  • The Portuguese built trading posts on the West African coast and grew sugar on Atlantic islands using enslaved Africans. That plantation model was later carried to the Americas.
  • Columbus sailed for Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain and landed in the Caribbean, believing he had reached Asia.
  • Later, joint-stock companies let English and Dutch investors pool money and share the risk of colonial ventures.

Practice 1.3 · 4 questions

1.4

1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest

  • The Columbian Exchange was the transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492.
  • To the Americas: horses, cattle, pigs, wheat, sugar cane, and diseases such as smallpox and measles. Epidemics killed a large share of the Native population.
  • To Europe, Africa, and Asia: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, and tobacco. The new food crops supported population growth.
  • Gold and silver from the Americas and expanded trade helped Europe shift from feudalism toward capitalism.
  • Spanish conquistadors toppled the Aztec Empire (Cortés, 1519–1521) and the Inca Empire (Pizarro, 1530s), helped by disease, steel weapons, horses, and Native allies.
  • Sugar became the most important plantation crop in the Americas and drove the demand for enslaved labor.
  • Horses spread north from Spanish settlements and later transformed hunting, travel, and warfare for Plains peoples.
  • Silver from mines such as Potosí flowed to Europe and Asia, expanded global trade, and contributed to rising prices in Europe.
  • In Africa, European demand for labor expanded the slave trade, strengthened some coastal states, and drained population from others.
  • In some regions the Native population fell by as much as 90 percent within a century of contact.

Practice 1.4 · 6 questions

1.5

1.5 Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System

  • Under the encomienda system, the Spanish crown granted colonists the right to demand labor and tribute from Native Americans in a given area, in return for supposedly protecting and Christianizing them. In practice it meant forced labor in fields and mines.
  • As disease and overwork reduced the Native population, and as the crown tried to limit abuses (the New Laws of 1542), the Spanish turned increasingly to enslaved Africans for plantation and mining labor.
  • The Spanish developed a casta system that ranked people by racial ancestry: Europeans born in Spain at the top, then American-born Spaniards, then people of mixed ancestry such as mestizos (Spanish and Native American), with Native Americans and Africans at the bottom.
  • Holders of encomiendas were called encomenderos. In the Andes the Spanish also adapted the Inca labor draft to force Native men to work in silver mines.
  • The New Laws of 1542 banned the enslavement of Native Americans and tried to phase out the encomienda. Colonists resisted, and enforcement was weak.
  • The encomienda was gradually replaced by other forced-labor systems and by large estates called haciendas.
  • Top to bottom, the casta ranks were peninsulares (born in Spain), creoles (Spaniards born in the Americas), people of mixed ancestry, and then Native Americans and Africans.
  • Most Spanish colonists were men, and marriage with Native and African women was common. The large mixed population set Spanish America apart from the later English colonies.

Practice 1.5 · 6 questions

1.6

1.6 Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans

  • Europeans and Native Americans held different views on religion, gender roles, family, land use, and power. Europeans treated land as private property; many Native societies treated it as a shared resource.
  • Contact brought misunderstanding and conflict, and also exchange: each side adopted useful goods and knowledge from the other.
  • Native peoples defended their sovereignty, economies, and beliefs through both diplomacy and military resistance.
  • Spaniards debated how Native Americans should be treated. Bartolomé de las Casas condemned Spanish cruelty and argued that Native Americans were fully human. Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that they were naturally inferior and that conquest was justified. The two argued their cases in the Valladolid debate (1550–1551).
  • Europeans developed belief systems that justified the subjugation of Africans and Native Americans.
  • Many Native societies held that the natural world was filled with spirits, and many gave women authority over farming and kinship. Europeans were Christian and patriarchal.
  • Early trade created mutual dependence. Europeans wanted furs, food, and knowledge of the land. Native peoples wanted metal tools, cloth, and firearms.
  • Native peoples and Africans often blended Christianity with their own beliefs, a process called syncretism.
  • In 1599 the Spanish under Juan de Oñate brutally crushed resistance at Acoma Pueblo in New Mexico.
  • Europeans justified conquest and slavery with claims of religious and cultural superiority.

Practice 1.6 · 5 questions

1.7

1.7 Causation in Period 1

  • Causes of exploration: competition among European states, the search for wealth and trade routes, religious zeal, and new technology.
  • Effects in the Americas: the Columbian Exchange, epidemic disease and population collapse, Spanish conquest, forced-labor systems, and the growth of the Atlantic slave trade.
  • Effects in Europe: new crops and population growth, new wealth, the growth of capitalism, and sharper rivalry as other states sought their own colonies.
  • Chain of causes: rivalry and the search for wealth led to exploration; contact led to the Columbian Exchange; disease and conquest led to labor shortages; labor shortages led to the Atlantic slave trade.
  • Slavery based on race in the Americas grew out of Spanish and Portuguese plantation and mining labor in this period.

Watch outFor causation questions, separate immediate effects from long-term effects, and be ready to say which cause mattered most and why.

Practice 1.7 · 4 questions

Unit 2 · 6–8% of exam

Period 2: 1607–1754

2.1

2.1 Contextualizing Period 2

  • Spain, France, the Netherlands, and England built colonies in North America with different goals, methods, and relations with Native peoples.
  • The British colonies grew quickly through migration and natural increase. They developed distinct regional economies, tied themselves to Atlantic trade, and came to rely on enslaved labor.
  • Colonists built habits of self-government while Britain enforced its rules loosely.
  • The period runs from the founding of Jamestown (1607) to the start of the French and Indian War (1754).
  • Dates to anchor the period: 1607 Jamestown; 1619 House of Burgesses meets and the first enslaved Africans arrive in Virginia; 1620 Plymouth; 1630 Massachusetts Bay; 1675–1676 Metacom's War and Bacon's Rebellion; 1680 Pueblo Revolt; 1688 Glorious Revolution; 1692 Salem witch trials; 1730s–1740s First Great Awakening; 1739 Stono Rebellion; 1754 French and Indian War begins.
  • The population of the British mainland colonies grew from a few thousand to more than one million by 1750.

Practice 2.1 · 4 questions

2.2

2.2 European Colonization

  • Spanish: sought wealth and converts. They built missions and forts, subjugated Native peoples, and brought them into colonial society. Settlements included St. Augustine (1565) and Santa Fe (1610).
  • French: few settlers. They relied on the fur trade, alliances, and intermarriage with American Indians. Quebec was founded in 1608.
  • Dutch: few settlers and a commercial focus. New Netherland was a trading colony centered on New Amsterdam; England seized it in 1664 and renamed it New York.
  • English: large numbers of men and women migrated, seeking land, economic opportunity, and religious freedom. They farmed, took land from Native peoples, and lived apart from them.
  • Jamestown was founded in 1607 by the Virginia Company, a joint-stock company. Most early settlers died of disease and hunger in the "starving time." John Rolfe's tobacco made the colony profitable.
  • The headright system gave 50 acres of land to anyone who paid for a settler's passage to Virginia, which rewarded planters who imported servants.
  • New France: Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec. French traders and Jesuit missionaries lived among American Indians and allied with the Huron and Algonquian peoples.
  • New Netherland: the Dutch West India Company ran the colony for trade and tolerated many religions to attract settlers.

Practice 2.2 · 7 questions

2.3

2.3 The Regions of British Colonies

  • Chesapeake (Virginia, Maryland) and North Carolina: tobacco, a labor-intensive cash crop. Workers were at first mostly male indentured servants, later enslaved Africans. The House of Burgesses (1619) was the first elected assembly in the English colonies. Maryland was founded as a refuge for Catholics.
  • New England: settled by Puritans who came as families. Small towns, family farms, and a mixed economy of farming, fishing, shipbuilding, and trade. Town meetings gave local self-government. Dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson were banished; Williams founded Rhode Island.
  • Middle colonies (New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware): exported grain. The most ethnically and religiously diverse region. William Penn founded Pennsylvania as a Quaker colony that practiced religious toleration.
  • Southern Atlantic coast and British West Indies: long growing seasons and plantations growing staple crops such as rice and sugar. Enslaved Africans were often the majority of the population.
  • Distance and loose British oversight let colonies create self-governing institutions that were unusually democratic for the time. In the South, elite planters dominated the assemblies.
  • Plymouth (1620) was founded by Separatist Pilgrims. In the Mayflower Compact they agreed to govern themselves by majority rule.
  • Massachusetts Bay (1630) was founded by Puritans who wanted to purify the Church of England. John Winthrop called the colony a "city upon a hill," a model for the world.
  • About 20,000 Puritans arrived in the 1630s. They valued literacy for reading the Bible and founded Harvard in 1636.
  • Roger Williams argued for separating church and state and founded Rhode Island. Anne Hutchinson challenged the ministers' authority and was banished. The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639) set up a representative government.
  • Maryland's Act of Toleration (1649) protected the worship of all Christians.
  • Pennsylvania was William Penn's "holy experiment." Quakers believed in equality and pacifism and dealt more fairly with American Indians.
  • Carolina was settled partly by planters from Barbados who brought enslaved Africans and a harsh slave code. Georgia (1732) was founded by James Oglethorpe as a buffer against Spanish Florida and a refuge for debtors.

Watch outKnow each region's economy, labor system, and settlers. Comparison questions about the regions are common.

Practice 2.3 · 11 questions

2.4

2.4 Transatlantic Trade

  • An Atlantic economy linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas through the exchange of goods, enslaved Africans and American Indians, and ideas. The pattern is often called the triangular trade.
  • Mercantilism held that colonies exist to enrich the home country: they supply raw materials and buy its manufactured goods.
  • The Navigation Acts (beginning in 1651) required trade to be carried on English or colonial ships and required certain colonial goods, such as tobacco and sugar, to be sent only to England.
  • Enforcement was loose and smuggling was common. This period of light British oversight is called salutary neglect.
  • Trade with Europeans brought new goods into American Indian communities and spread epidemic diseases.
  • In one common pattern of triangular trade, New England ships carried rum to West Africa, enslaved Africans to the West Indies on the Middle Passage, and sugar and molasses back to New England.
  • The Navigation Acts also helped the colonies by protecting their shipping and guaranteeing markets, but colonists resented the limits and often smuggled.
  • The Dominion of New England (1686–1689) merged the New England colonies under a royal governor, Sir Edmund Andros, and ended their assemblies. It collapsed after the Glorious Revolution in England.
  • By the 1700s colonists were buying large amounts of British manufactured goods.

Practice 2.4 · 6 questions

2.5

2.5 Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

  • Relations mixed accommodation and conflict. European powers allied with and armed American Indian groups, who in turn used those alliances against Native rivals.
  • British colonists fought American Indians over land, resources, and boundaries. In Metacom's War (King Philip's War, 1675–1676), the Wampanoag leader Metacom and his allies attacked New England towns; their defeat broke Native power in southern New England.
  • In the Pueblo Revolt (1680), Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for more than a decade. After returning, the Spanish accommodated some aspects of Pueblo culture.
  • Trade in furs and guns changed Native economies and intensified warfare among Native groups.
  • Virginia: the Powhatan Confederacy first traded with Jamestown, then fought it. An attack in 1622 killed about a quarter of the colonists, and by 1646 the Powhatan had been defeated.
  • Pequot War (1636–1638): New England colonists and their Native allies nearly destroyed the Pequot.
  • Bacon's Rebellion (1676): Nathaniel Bacon led frontier farmers and former servants against Governor William Berkeley, who had refused to back attacks on American Indians. The rebels burned Jamestown.
  • The Iroquois Confederacy gained power by trading furs and playing the French and English against each other.
  • The Pueblo Revolt, led by Popé, was caused by forced labor, drought, and Spanish suppression of Pueblo religion.

Practice 2.5 · 7 questions

2.6

2.6 Slavery in the British Colonies

  • All British colonies took part in the Atlantic slave trade, driven by abundant land, European demand for colonial goods, and a shortage of indentured servants.
  • New England held relatively few enslaved people. The Chesapeake and the southern Atlantic coast held many. The great majority of enslaved Africans were sent to the West Indies.
  • Bacon's Rebellion (1676) showed Chesapeake planters the danger of a large class of discontented former servants and sped the shift to enslaved African labor.
  • Chattel slavery treated people as property. Laws made slavery hereditary through the mother and created a strict racial system that banned interracial relationships.
  • Enslaved people resisted overtly, as in the Stono Rebellion (South Carolina, 1739), and covertly, by working slowly, breaking tools, running away, and preserving family ties, culture, and religion.
  • In 1619 about twenty enslaved Africans were brought to Virginia, the first recorded in the English mainland colonies.
  • As the supply of enslaved Africans rose and the supply of English servants fell in the late 1600s, slavery replaced servitude in the Chesapeake.
  • Slave codes, such as Virginia's of 1705, defined enslaved people as property and restricted their movement, assembly, and learning.
  • On Carolina rice plantations, enslaved people often worked under a task system and kept more African customs. The Gullah language and culture developed there.
  • Spanish Florida offered freedom to people who escaped from the English colonies, which encouraged the Stono rebels to march south.
  • Some Quakers were among the first colonists to condemn slavery.

Practice 2.6 · 8 questions

2.7

2.7 Colonial Society and Culture

  • The First Great Awakening (1730s–1740s) was a wave of Protestant revivals led by preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield. It stressed emotional, personal faith, split churches, and encouraged people to question established authority. It was a shared experience across the colonies.
  • The Enlightenment stressed reason and natural rights. John Locke argued that people have natural rights and that government rests on the consent of the governed. Benjamin Franklin embodied Enlightenment thinking in the colonies.
  • Anglicization: the colonies became more like Britain in their political institutions, law, trade, print culture, and Protestant religion.
  • The Zenger trial (1735) was an early victory for freedom of the press.
  • Colonists' resistance to imperial control drew on their experience of self-government, ideas of liberty, the Enlightenment, religious independence, and a belief that the imperial system was corrupt.
  • Jonathan Edwards preached "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God." George Whitefield toured the colonies and drew huge crowds. Supporters of the revivals were called New Lights and opponents Old Lights.
  • The Great Awakening led to new colleges, including Princeton, and to the growth of Baptist and Presbyterian churches.
  • Benjamin Franklin published Poor Richard's Almanack, experimented with electricity, and promoted practical learning.
  • Colonial government: an appointed governor, a council, and an elected assembly. Assemblies controlled taxes and spending, the power of the purse. Voting was limited to white men who owned property.
  • Population roughly doubled every 25 years. Germans settled in Pennsylvania and Scots-Irish migrants settled the backcountry.
  • Colonial society had no hereditary nobility and offered white men more social mobility than Europe did. Married women had few legal rights.

Practice 2.7 · 9 questions

2.8

2.8 Comparison in Period 2

  • Chesapeake versus New England: the Chesapeake was settled for profit, mostly by young single men, on scattered tobacco farms, with high death rates and a growing reliance on enslaved labor. New England was settled for religious reasons by families in towns, with a mixed economy and longer lives.
  • Empires: the Spanish converted and subjugated Native peoples; the French and Dutch traded and allied with them; the English came in large numbers and displaced them.
  • Similarities among the British colonies: an English political heritage, elected assemblies, a Protestant majority, participation in Atlantic trade, and conflict with American Indians over land.
  • Spanish and English colonies: Spanish colonies were tightly controlled by the crown and the Catholic Church and brought Native peoples into colonial society. English colonies were founded by companies and proprietors, governed themselves through assemblies, and pushed Native peoples out.
  • Two revolts: after the Pueblo Revolt the Spanish made lasting concessions. After Metacom's War the English made none, and Native power in southern New England was destroyed.
  • Labor: New England relied on family labor, the Chesapeake on indentured servants and then enslaved Africans, and the Carolina and West Indies plantations on enslaved Africans from the start.

Watch outA strong comparison names a specific similarity or difference and explains the reason for it, such as environment, settlers' goals, or the labor system.

Practice 2.8 · 5 questions

Unit 3 · 10–17% of exam

Period 3: 1754–1800

3.1

3.1 Contextualizing Period 3

  • Britain's victory over France in 1763 left it with a huge debt and a larger empire, so it ended its loose oversight of the colonies and tried to tax and control them.
  • Colonists, used to governing themselves, resisted. Resistance grew into a war for independence and then into an experiment in republican government.
  • The new nation argued over how strong its central government should be, how to deal with Britain and France, and what to do about slavery and American Indian land.
  • Dates to anchor the period: 1754 French and Indian War begins; 1763 Treaty of Paris and Proclamation Line; 1765 Stamp Act; 1776 Declaration of Independence; 1781 Yorktown and Articles of Confederation; 1787 Constitutional Convention; 1789 Washington inaugurated; 1800 Jefferson elected.

Practice 3.1 · 2 questions

3.2

3.2 The Seven Years' War (The French and Indian War)

  • Britain and France fought for control of the Ohio River Valley. Most American Indian nations sided with the French, who were traders and not land-hungry settlers.
  • At the Albany Congress (1754), Benjamin Franklin proposed the Albany Plan of Union for a common colonial defense. The colonies rejected it.
  • The Treaty of Paris of 1763 removed France from North America. Britain gained Canada and all land east of the Mississippi River.
  • Pontiac's Rebellion (1763) led Britain to issue the Proclamation of 1763, which barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains. Colonists resented it.
  • The war doubled Britain's debt. Parliament decided the colonies should help pay for their own defense.

Practice 3.2 · 3 questions

3.3

3.3 Taxation Without Representation

  • The Stamp Act (1765) was the first direct tax on the colonists. They answered with the Stamp Act Congress, boycotts, and groups such as the Sons of Liberty. Parliament repealed it but declared its right to legislate for the colonies.
  • Colonists argued that only their own assemblies could tax them. Britain answered that Parliament represented all subjects (virtual representation).
  • The Townshend Acts (1767) taxed imported goods such as glass, paper, and tea. Colonists boycotted British goods, and women made homespun cloth.
  • The Boston Massacre (1770) and the Boston Tea Party (1773) raised tensions. Britain punished Massachusetts with the Coercive (Intolerable) Acts in 1774.
  • Committees of correspondence linked the colonies, and the First Continental Congress met in 1774.

Practice 3.3 · 3 questions

3.4

3.4 Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution

  • Colonists drew on the Enlightenment: people have natural rights, and government exists by the consent of the governed.
  • Republicanism held that a nation should be governed by its citizens through elected representatives, with no king or nobility, and that citizens must put the common good first.
  • Thomas Paine's _Common Sense_ (January 1776) attacked monarchy in plain language and argued for independence.
  • The Declaration of Independence (July 1776), written mainly by Thomas Jefferson, stated that all men are created equal, that they have rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and that people may replace a government that violates their rights.

Practice 3.4 · 2 questions

3.5

3.5 The American Revolution

  • Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. The Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army under George Washington.
  • Colonists were divided among Patriots, Loyalists, and people who tried to stay neutral.
  • The American victory at Saratoga (1777) convinced France to form an alliance in 1778. French money, troops, and ships were decisive.
  • The British surrender at Yorktown (1781) ended major fighting. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized independence and set the western boundary at the Mississippi River.
  • The Patriots won despite Britain's stronger army and navy because of Washington's leadership, foreign aid, knowledge of the land, and commitment to their cause.

Practice 3.5 · 3 questions

3.6

3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals

  • Talk of liberty and equality led many to question slavery. Northern states began gradual emancipation, while slavery expanded in the South.
  • Republican motherhood held that women should be educated so they could raise virtuous citizens. Women's political rights did not expand, though Abigail Adams urged her husband to "remember the ladies."
  • State constitutions and new laws reduced property requirements for voting and ended some established churches.
  • The American Revolution inspired later revolutions in France, Haiti, and Latin America.

Practice 3.6 · 2 questions

3.7

3.7 The Articles of Confederation

  • The Articles of Confederation (ratified 1781) created a weak central government because Americans feared a distant, powerful authority.
  • Congress could not tax, could not regulate trade between states, and had no executive or national courts. Each state had one vote, and amendments required all thirteen states to agree.
  • Its main success was western land policy. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 set up a process for territories to become states, banned slavery in the Northwest Territory, and promoted public education.
  • Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787), an uprising of indebted Massachusetts farmers, convinced many leaders that a stronger national government was needed.

Practice 3.7 · 3 questions

3.8

3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification

  • Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 to revise the Articles and wrote a new constitution instead.
  • The Great Compromise created a two-house Congress: representation by population in the House (as in the Virginia Plan) and equal representation in the Senate (as in the New Jersey Plan).
  • The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three-fifths of enslaved people for representation and taxation. Congress could not ban the international slave trade until 1808.
  • Federalists supported ratification. Hamilton, Madison, and Jay argued for it in the _Federalist Papers_. Anti-Federalists feared a strong central government and demanded a bill of rights.
  • The Constitution was ratified in 1788 after Federalists promised to add a Bill of Rights, which was ratified in 1791.

Practice 3.8 · 3 questions

3.9

3.9 The Constitution

  • Federalism divides power between the national government and the states.
  • Separation of powers divides the national government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches.
  • Checks and balances let each branch limit the others: the president can veto laws, Congress can override vetoes and impeach, and courts can rule on laws.
  • The Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments, protects individual liberties such as speech, religion, and trial by jury, and reserves other powers to the states and the people.

Practice 3.9 · 2 questions

3.10

3.10 Shaping a New Republic

  • Washington set precedents, including the cabinet and serving two terms.
  • Hamilton's financial plan: the national government would take over state debts, create a national bank, and raise money through tariffs and an excise tax on whiskey. Jefferson and Madison opposed it as favoring the wealthy and exceeding the Constitution.
  • The Whiskey Rebellion (1794) was put down by federal troops, which showed the new government's strength.
  • The first parties formed. Federalists (Hamilton) wanted a strong central government, commerce, and ties with Britain. Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson, Madison) wanted states' rights, an agrarian nation, and sympathy for France.
  • Foreign policy: the Proclamation of Neutrality (1793), Jay's Treaty with Britain, and Pinckney's Treaty with Spain. Washington's Farewell Address warned against permanent alliances and political parties.
  • Under John Adams, the Alien and Sedition Acts (1798) limited criticism of the government. The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions answered that states could judge federal laws unconstitutional.

Practice 3.10 · 4 questions

3.11

3.11 Developing an American Identity

  • After independence, Americans worked to create a national culture in art, literature, and architecture that expressed republican ideals.
  • Ideas about national identity developed alongside strong regional identities and loyalties to states.
  • Enlightenment ideas and religious liberty shaped the culture. Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom (1786) separated church and state there.
  • Many groups were left out of the new identity, including women, enslaved people, and American Indians.

Practice 3.11 · 1 question

3.12

3.12 Movement in the Early Republic

  • Settlers poured west across the Appalachians, which led to wars with American Indians. After the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794), the Treaty of Greenville opened most of Ohio to settlement.
  • Frontier settlers often resented eastern elites, as in the Whiskey Rebellion.
  • Spain expanded its missions into California, bringing more contact and conflict with Native peoples there.
  • The cotton gin (1793) made cotton highly profitable and spread slavery westward, even as northern states were ending it. Antislavery feeling grew in the North.

Practice 3.12 · 2 questions

3.13

3.13 Continuity and Change in Period 3

  • Changes: independence from Britain, written constitutions, republican government, a stronger federal system, the first political parties, and gradual abolition in the North.
  • Continuities: slavery remained and expanded in the South, women lacked political rights, voting stayed limited mostly to white men with property, and pressure on American Indian land continued.

Watch outFor continuity and change questions, name one thing that changed and one that stayed the same, with a specific example of each.

Practice 3.13 · 2 questions

Unit 4 · 10–17% of exam

Period 4: 1800–1848

4.1

4.1 Contextualizing Period 4

  • The young republic expanded its territory, its democracy, and its market economy.
  • New technology and transportation tied regions together economically, while slavery increasingly divided them.
  • Religious revivals and reform movements tried to improve American society.
  • Dates to anchor the period: 1800 Jefferson elected; 1803 Louisiana Purchase and Marbury v. Madison; 1812–1815 War of 1812; 1820 Missouri Compromise; 1823 Monroe Doctrine; 1825 Erie Canal opens; 1828 Jackson elected; 1830 Indian Removal Act; 1848 Seneca Falls Convention.

Practice 4.1 · 1 question

4.2

4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson

  • The election of 1800 was the first peaceful transfer of power between parties, from Federalists to Democratic-Republicans.
  • In _Marbury v. Madison_ (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall established judicial review, the Supreme Court's power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution.
  • The Louisiana Purchase (1803) doubled the size of the country. Jefferson, who read the Constitution strictly, bought it even though the Constitution did not mention buying territory. Lewis and Clark explored it.
  • The Marshall Court strengthened federal power. _McCulloch v. Maryland_ (1819) upheld the national bank and barred states from taxing it. _Gibbons v. Ogden_ (1824) gave Congress control of interstate commerce.

Practice 4.2 · 3 questions

4.3

4.3 Politics and Regional Interests

  • British seizure of American ships and sailors (impressment) and support for American Indian resistance led to the War of 1812. Earlier, Jefferson's Embargo Act (1807) had tried to avoid war and hurt American trade instead.
  • New England Federalists who opposed the war met at the Hartford Convention. After the war they looked disloyal, and the party collapsed.
  • Henry Clay's American System called for a protective tariff, a national bank, and federally funded roads and canals.
  • The Missouri Compromise (1820) admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, and banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of 36°30′.
  • Regional interests clashed: the North favored tariffs, the South opposed them, and the West wanted internal improvements and cheap land.

Practice 4.3 · 3 questions

4.4

4.4 America on the World Stage

  • The War of 1812 ended with the Treaty of Ghent, which changed no boundaries. Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans made him a national hero and fed a surge of nationalism.
  • In the Adams–Onís Treaty (1819), Spain gave Florida to the United States.
  • The Monroe Doctrine (1823) declared the Western Hemisphere closed to new European colonization and promised that the United States would stay out of European affairs.
  • The United States sought to expand its trade and its borders, and to keep European powers out of the Americas.

Practice 4.4 · 2 questions

4.5

4.5 Market Revolution: Industrialization

  • The market revolution changed how goods were made and moved: people produced for distant markets and not just for themselves.
  • Textile mills, such as those at Lowell, Massachusetts, brought spinning and weaving into factories. Interchangeable parts made mass production possible.
  • Transportation: steamboats, the Erie Canal (1825), which linked the Great Lakes to New York City, and then railroads cut the cost and time of shipping. The telegraph sped communication.
  • Farm inventions such as the steel plow and mechanical reaper raised output.
  • New links tied the North and the Midwest together more closely than either was tied to the South.

Practice 4.5 · 3 questions

4.6

4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture

  • Large numbers of immigrants from Ireland (fleeing famine) and Germany arrived in the 1840s. Many Irish settled in northeastern cities and worked in factories and on canals.
  • Cities grew quickly, and so did the gap between rich and poor. A new middle class of shopkeepers, clerks, and professionals emerged.
  • Work moved out of the home. The cult of domesticity taught that women's proper sphere was the home and family, while men worked for wages.
  • Young women who worked in the Lowell mills lived in boardinghouses and at times organized against wage cuts.

Practice 4.6 · 2 questions

4.7

4.7 Expanding Democracy

  • By the 1820s most states had dropped property requirements, so nearly all white men could vote. Women, American Indians, and most Black men could not.
  • In the election of 1824, John Quincy Adams won in the House of Representatives after Henry Clay backed him. Jackson's supporters called it a "corrupt bargain."
  • Andrew Jackson won in 1828 as the champion of the "common man." Campaigns began to use rallies, slogans, and party organization.
  • Jackson rewarded supporters with government jobs, the spoils system.
  • New parties formed: Jackson's Democrats and their opponents, the Whigs.

Practice 4.7 · 2 questions

4.8

4.8 Jackson and Federal Power

  • The Indian Removal Act (1830) authorized moving southeastern nations west of the Mississippi. In _Worcester v. Georgia_ the Supreme Court sided with the Cherokee, but Jackson did not enforce the ruling. The forced march of the Cherokee in 1838 is called the Trail of Tears.
  • In the Nullification Crisis (1832–1833), South Carolina, led by John C. Calhoun, declared a federal tariff void. Jackson threatened force, and a compromise tariff ended the crisis.
  • In the Bank War, Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States, calling it a tool of the wealthy. He moved federal money to state banks.
  • Opponents who saw Jackson as abusing presidential power formed the Whig Party.

Practice 4.8 · 3 questions

4.9

4.9 The Development of an American Culture

  • A national culture took shape that mixed American subjects with European influences.
  • Transcendentalists such as Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau stressed individual conscience, self-reliance, and nature. Thoreau argued for civil disobedience against unjust laws.
  • Painters of the Hudson River School celebrated the American landscape.
  • Utopian communities, such as Brook Farm, Oneida, and the Shakers, tried to build perfect societies based on shared property or new social rules.

Practice 4.9 · 2 questions

4.10

4.10 The Second Great Awakening

  • The Second Great Awakening was a wave of Protestant revivals in the early 1800s, with large camp meetings and preachers such as Charles Finney.
  • It taught that individuals could choose salvation and could improve themselves and society.
  • Methodist and Baptist churches grew fastest. New groups appeared, including the Mormons, founded by Joseph Smith.
  • The revivals inspired many of the era's reform movements, and women took a leading part.

Practice 4.10 · 2 questions

4.11

4.11 An Age of Reform

  • Temperance reformers tried to limit alcohol.
  • Abolition: William Lloyd Garrison's newspaper _The Liberator_ (1831) demanded an immediate end to slavery. Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery, became a leading speaker and writer.
  • Women's rights: at the Seneca Falls Convention (1848), Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott issued the Declaration of Sentiments, which demanded equality and the vote.
  • Education: Horace Mann promoted free public schools. Dorothea Dix worked for better treatment of people with mental illness.
  • Abolitionists were a minority in the North, and their demands angered the South.

Practice 4.11 · 3 questions

4.12

4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic

  • Free Black communities in northern cities built their own institutions, such as the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and worked against slavery. They still faced discrimination and limits on voting.
  • Enslaved people preserved families, religion, and culture, and resisted through work slowdowns, escape, and revolt.
  • Nat Turner's Rebellion (Virginia, 1831) killed about sixty white people. Southern states answered with harsher slave codes and limits on teaching enslaved people to read.
  • Plots led by Gabriel (1800) and Denmark Vesey (1822) were discovered before they began.

Practice 4.12 · 2 questions

4.13

4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic

  • Cotton became the South's main crop, and the region was called the Cotton Kingdom. Planters moved southwest into Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana.
  • After the international slave trade ended in 1808, a large internal slave trade moved enslaved people from the upper South to the cotton states and broke up families.
  • Most white southerners owned no slaves, but a small class of wealthy planters dominated society and politics.
  • Southern leaders such as John C. Calhoun came to defend slavery as a "positive good" and not merely a necessary evil.
  • The South had few cities, factories, or immigrants compared with the North.

Practice 4.13 · 2 questions

4.14

4.14 Causation in Period 4

  • The market revolution caused the growth of cities, a middle class, and regional specialization, and it bound North and West together.
  • Wider suffrage for white men caused new parties and a new style of politics.
  • The Second Great Awakening caused reform movements.
  • Cotton and westward expansion caused the spread of slavery and growing conflict between the sections.

Practice 4.14 · 2 questions

Unit 5 · 10–17% of exam

Period 5: 1844–1877

5.1

5.1 Contextualizing Period 5

  • Expansion to the Pacific reopened the question of whether slavery would spread into new territory.
  • Compromises failed during the 1850s, and the election of Abraham Lincoln led to secession and civil war.
  • Union victory ended slavery and preserved the nation. Reconstruction then tried, with limited success, to secure rights for formerly enslaved people.
  • Dates to anchor the period: 1846–1848 Mexican–American War; 1850 Compromise of 1850; 1854 Kansas–Nebraska Act; 1857 Dred Scott decision; 1860 Lincoln elected; 1861–1865 Civil War; 1863 Emancipation Proclamation; 1865 Thirteenth Amendment; 1877 Reconstruction ends.

Practice 5.1 · 2 questions

5.2

5.2 Manifest Destiny

  • Manifest Destiny was the belief that the United States was meant to spread across the continent, bringing its institutions with it.
  • Settlers followed the Oregon Trail to the Pacific Northwest. The United States and Britain divided the Oregon Country at the 49th parallel in 1846.
  • Texas, which had won independence from Mexico in 1836, was annexed in 1845.
  • The California Gold Rush (1849) drew a flood of migrants. Expansion brought conflict with American Indians and Mexicans already living in the West.

Practice 5.2 · 2 questions

5.3

5.3 The Mexican–American War

  • President James K. Polk wanted California and the Southwest. A clash in disputed territory along the Rio Grande led to war in 1846.
  • In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848), Mexico gave up California and most of the present-day Southwest, the Mexican Cession, for $15 million.
  • The Wilmot Proviso proposed banning slavery in any land taken from Mexico. It passed the House but not the Senate and inflamed sectional feeling.
  • Mexicans and American Indians in the new territory were promised rights, but many lost land and political power.

Practice 5.3 · 2 questions

5.4

5.4 The Compromise of 1850

  • California's request to enter as a free state threatened the balance between free and slave states.
  • The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state, let the Utah and New Mexico territories decide on slavery by popular sovereignty, ended the slave trade in Washington, D.C., and passed a stronger Fugitive Slave Act.
  • The Fugitive Slave Act required northerners to help return people who had escaped slavery. It angered the North and strengthened the antislavery movement.

Practice 5.4 · 2 questions

5.5

5.5 Sectional Conflict: Regional Differences

  • The North had a growing population, factories, railroads, and a free-labor ideal: the belief that people should be free to work for wages and rise.
  • Irish and German immigration led to nativism. The anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic Know-Nothing party was briefly powerful.
  • Abolitionists were a minority, but _Uncle Tom's Cabin_ (1852) by Harriet Beecher Stowe turned many northerners against slavery. The Underground Railroad helped people escape.
  • The South remained agricultural and dependent on enslaved labor, and its leaders defended slavery and states' rights.

Practice 5.5 · 2 questions

5.6

5.6 Failure of Compromise

  • The Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854) let those territories decide on slavery by popular sovereignty, which repealed the Missouri Compromise line. Proslavery and antislavery settlers fought in "Bleeding Kansas."
  • The Republican Party formed in 1854 to oppose the spread of slavery into the territories.
  • In _Dred Scott v. Sandford_ (1857), the Supreme Court ruled that Black Americans were not citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.
  • In the Lincoln–Douglas debates (1858), Lincoln argued against the spread of slavery. John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry (1859) terrified the South.

Practice 5.6 · 3 questions

5.7

5.7 Election of 1860 and Secession

  • The Democratic Party split into northern and southern wings. Abraham Lincoln, the Republican, won the presidency in 1860 without carrying a single southern state.
  • Lincoln opposed the spread of slavery but said he would not interfere with it where it existed. Southern leaders did not believe him.
  • South Carolina seceded in December 1860, and other Deep South states followed. They formed the Confederate States of America.
  • The war began when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861. Four more states then seceded. The slaveholding border states stayed in the Union.

Practice 5.7 · 2 questions

5.8

5.8 Military Conflict in the Civil War

  • The Union had more people, factories, railroads, and a navy. The Confederacy had skilled generals, a defensive war on familiar ground, and hopes of European help.
  • The Union plan was to blockade southern ports, take control of the Mississippi River, and capture Richmond.
  • Antietam (1862) stopped a Confederate invasion and gave Lincoln the chance to announce emancipation.
  • In July 1863, Union victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg turned the war. Vicksburg gave the Union control of the Mississippi.
  • Sherman's March to the Sea destroyed southern resources. Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox in April 1865.

Practice 5.8 · 3 questions

5.9

5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War

  • The Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863) declared free the enslaved people in areas in rebellion. It did not apply to the border states. It made ending slavery a war aim, discouraged European support for the Confederacy, and opened the army to Black soldiers.
  • About 200,000 African Americans served in the Union army and navy.
  • In the Gettysburg Address, Lincoln described the war as a struggle to preserve a nation dedicated to equality.
  • With southerners gone from Congress, Republicans passed the Homestead Act, the Pacific Railway Act, and the Morrill Land-Grant Act (all 1862).
  • Lincoln suspended habeas corpus in some areas, and both sides drafted soldiers. The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery.

Practice 5.9 · 3 questions

5.10

5.10 Reconstruction

  • Reconstruction (1865–1877) dealt with how to readmit the southern states and what rights formerly enslaved people would have.
  • The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery. The Fourteenth granted citizenship and equal protection of the laws. The Fifteenth said the vote could not be denied because of race.
  • President Andrew Johnson was lenient toward the South. Southern states passed Black Codes that restricted freedpeople.
  • Radical Republicans in Congress took control, placed the South under military rule, and required new state constitutions. The House impeached Johnson, and the Senate fell one vote short of removing him.
  • The Freedmen's Bureau provided food, schools, and legal help. Black men voted and held office.
  • The women's rights movement split over the Fifteenth Amendment because it did not include women.

Practice 5.10 · 3 questions

5.11

5.11 Failure of Reconstruction

  • Most freedpeople got no land. Many became sharecroppers, farming a planter's land for a share of the crop and falling into debt.
  • White supremacist groups such as the Ku Klux Klan used violence to keep Black southerners from voting.
  • Northern support faded because of economic depression, corruption scandals, and weariness.
  • In the Compromise of 1877, Republican Rutherford B. Hayes became president after a disputed election, and federal troops left the South. Reconstruction ended.
  • Southern governments then stripped Black citizens of rights, but the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments remained as a basis for later civil rights victories.

Practice 5.11 · 3 questions

5.12

5.12 Comparison in Period 5

  • North and South in the war: the North had industry, population, and railroads; the South had cotton, defensive strategy, and military leadership.
  • Plans for Reconstruction: Lincoln and Johnson wanted quick readmission; Radical Republicans wanted to remake the South and protect freedpeople.
  • Compromises: the Missouri Compromise drew a line; the Compromise of 1850 and the Kansas–Nebraska Act relied on popular sovereignty. Each delayed conflict, and none settled it.

Practice 5.12 · 2 questions
