AP United States History 2 · Units 6–9

APUSH 2 notes

NotesPractice · 113 questions

Unit 6 · 10–17% of exam

Period 6: 1865–1898

6.1

6.1 Contextualizing Period 6

  • After the Civil War the United States became an industrial power. Railroads, new technology, big business, and cheap labor drove rapid growth. The era is called the Gilded Age: glittering wealth on the surface, with poverty and corruption underneath.
  • Settlers, railroads, and the army pushed across the West and forced American Indians onto reservations.
  • Millions of immigrants and rural Americans moved to cities. Workers, farmers, and reformers challenged the power of corporations.
  • Dates to anchor the period: 1869 transcontinental railroad completed; 1877 Great Railroad Strike; 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act; 1887 Dawes Act and Interstate Commerce Act; 1890 Sherman Antitrust Act and Wounded Knee; 1892 Populist Party; 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson and McKinley elected.

Practice 6.1 · 2 questions

6.2

6.2 Westward Expansion: Economic Development

  • The first transcontinental railroad was finished in 1869, built largely by Chinese and Irish workers with federal land grants and loans. Railroads opened the West to settlement and national markets.
  • The Homestead Act drew farmers to the Great Plains. Mining and cattle ranching boomed.
  • New machinery raised farm output, but crop prices fell. Farmers faced high railroad rates and debt.
  • Farmers organized in the Grange and the Farmers' Alliances to demand regulation of railroads and cheaper credit.

Practice 6.2 · 2 questions

6.3

6.3 Westward Expansion: Social and Cultural Development

  • The government forced American Indians onto reservations. The army and Plains nations fought a series of wars, including the Sioux and Cheyenne victory at Little Bighorn (1876).
  • The near extinction of the bison destroyed the basis of Plains life.
  • The Dawes Act (1887) broke up reservation land into individual family plots to push American Indians to live as farmers. Much of the land ended up in white hands.
  • Boarding schools tried to erase Native languages and cultures. The army's killing of Lakota at Wounded Knee (1890) marked the end of armed resistance.
  • Many American Indians preserved their cultures and identities despite these policies.

Practice 6.3 · 2 questions

6.4

6.4 The "New South"

  • Boosters such as Henry Grady called for a "New South" of factories and cities. Textile mills, tobacco plants, and steel grew, but the region stayed mostly agricultural and poor, with sharecropping widespread.
  • In _Plessy v. Ferguson_ (1896) the Supreme Court upheld segregation under the rule of "separate but equal."
  • Jim Crow laws segregated public life. Poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence kept Black southerners from voting.
  • Booker T. Washington urged Black Americans to build economic strength through vocational education before demanding equality. Ida B. Wells led a campaign against lynching. W. E. B. Du Bois later demanded full civil rights at once.

Practice 6.4 · 3 questions

6.5

6.5 Technological Innovation

  • The Bessemer process made steel cheap, which made possible railroads, bridges, and skyscrapers.
  • Electricity lit cities and powered factories. Thomas Edison developed a practical light bulb and power systems.
  • The telephone (Alexander Graham Bell) and the telegraph sped communication.
  • New technology raised production, lowered prices, and created national markets for mass-produced goods.

Practice 6.5 · 2 questions

6.6

6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism

  • Business leaders built huge companies. Andrew Carnegie dominated steel by controlling every stage of production (vertical integration). John D. Rockefeller dominated oil by buying out competitors (horizontal integration) and forming a trust.
  • Supporters of laissez-faire said government should leave business alone. Social Darwinism claimed that the rich had succeeded because they were the fittest.
  • In the Gospel of Wealth, Carnegie argued that the rich had a duty to use their fortunes for the public good.
  • Critics called these men robber barons. The economy grew enormously, and so did the gap between rich and poor.

Practice 6.6 · 3 questions

6.7

6.7 Labor in the Gilded Age

  • Industrial workers faced low pay, long hours, dangerous conditions, and child labor.
  • The Knights of Labor welcomed nearly all workers, skilled and unskilled. The American Federation of Labor, led by Samuel Gompers, organized skilled workers and focused on wages, hours, and working conditions.
  • Major strikes included the Great Railroad Strike (1877), the Homestead Strike (1892), and the Pullman Strike (1894).
  • Government usually sided with employers, sending troops and issuing court orders against strikers.

Practice 6.7 · 2 questions

6.8

6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

  • After 1880, "new immigrants" came mainly from southern and eastern Europe: Italians, Poles, Russian Jews, and others. Chinese immigrants came to the West.
  • Most settled in cities, in crowded tenements and ethnic neighborhoods, and took industrial jobs.
  • Urban political machines, such as New York's Tammany Hall, gave immigrants jobs and help in exchange for votes, and were often corrupt.
  • African Americans began leaving the South. Some, called Exodusters, moved to Kansas.

Practice 6.8 · 2 questions

6.9

6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

  • Nativists claimed immigrants took jobs and threatened American culture.
  • The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) banned Chinese laborers. It was the first federal law to bar immigrants by nationality.
  • Settlement houses, such as Jane Addams's Hull House in Chicago, offered immigrants classes, child care, and other help.
  • Many reformers pushed immigrants to adopt American customs. Immigrants also kept their own languages, religions, and traditions.

Practice 6.9 · 2 questions

6.10

6.10 Development of the Middle Class

  • Corporations needed managers, clerks, and salespeople, which created a growing middle class of white-collar workers. Many clerical jobs went to women.
  • With more income and free time, people spent on leisure: spectator sports, vaudeville, amusement parks, and department stores.
  • Wealthy donors, following the Gospel of Wealth, funded libraries, universities, and museums.

Practice 6.10 · 1 question

6.11

6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age

  • The Social Gospel taught that Christians had a duty to fix social problems such as poverty.
  • Writers proposed alternatives to unregulated capitalism. Henry George called for a tax on land, and Edward Bellamy imagined a cooperative society.
  • Women led many reforms. The Woman's Christian Temperance Union fought alcohol, and the National American Woman Suffrage Association (1890) worked for the vote.
  • Some workers and thinkers turned to socialism.

Practice 6.11 · 2 questions

6.12

6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age

  • Most leaders favored laissez-faire, but farmers, workers, and small businesses demanded regulation.
  • The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) created a federal commission to regulate railroad rates. It was the first federal regulation of an industry.
  • The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) outlawed combinations that restrained trade. It was weakly enforced and at first was used more against unions than against corporations.

Practice 6.12 · 2 questions

6.13

6.13 Politics in the Gilded Age

  • Politics was closely contested and often corrupt. Parties rewarded supporters with government jobs until the Pendleton Civil Service Act (1883) required exams for many federal positions.
  • Major issues were tariffs and the money supply. Farmers and debtors wanted free silver to raise prices. Bankers and business wanted the gold standard.
  • The Populist Party (1892) called for free silver, a graduated income tax, government ownership of railroads, and direct election of senators.
  • In 1896 Democrat William Jennings Bryan, backed by the Populists, gave his "Cross of Gold" speech and lost to Republican William McKinley.

Practice 6.13 · 3 questions

6.14

6.14 Continuity and Change in Period 6

  • Changes: an industrial economy, national corporations, large cities, mass immigration, the end of the frontier, and the first federal regulation of business.
  • Continuities: racial discrimination and segregation, government support for business over labor, and conflict over American Indian land.

Practice 6.14 · 2 questions

Unit 7 · 10–17% of exam

Period 7: 1890–1945

7.1

7.1 Contextualizing Period 7

  • The United States became a world power, acquiring overseas territory and fighting in two world wars.
  • At home, Progressive reformers and then the New Deal expanded the role of the federal government in the economy and in people's lives.
  • The economy swung from the boom of the 1920s to the Great Depression and then to wartime prosperity.
  • Dates to anchor the period: 1898 Spanish–American War; 1917 United States enters World War I; 1920 Nineteenth Amendment; 1929 stock market crash; 1933 New Deal begins; 1941 Pearl Harbor; 1945 World War II ends.

Practice 7.1 · 2 questions

7.2

7.2 Imperialism: Debates

  • Imperialists argued that the United States needed overseas markets and raw materials, naval bases (as Alfred Thayer Mahan urged), and a share of world power. Some claimed a duty to spread American civilization, an idea tied to beliefs in racial superiority.
  • The census of 1890 reported that the frontier had closed, which made some look abroad.
  • Anti-imperialists, including Mark Twain and William Jennings Bryan, argued that ruling other peoples without their consent violated American principles of self-government.

Practice 7.2 · 2 questions

7.3

7.3 The Spanish–American War

  • Americans sympathized with Cuba's revolt against Spain. Sensational yellow journalism and the explosion of the battleship _Maine_ in Havana harbor pushed the country to war in 1898.
  • The war lasted a few months. Spain gave the United States Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines. Cuba became independent, but the Platt Amendment let the United States intervene there.
  • Filipinos who wanted independence fought a long, bloody war against American rule.
  • The Open Door policy sought equal trading rights in China. The Roosevelt Corollary claimed a right to police Latin America, and the United States built the Panama Canal.

Practice 7.3 · 3 questions

7.4

7.4 The Progressives

  • Progressives were reformers, mostly middle class and urban, who wanted government to fix the problems of industrial society.
  • Muckrakers exposed abuses. Upton Sinclair's _The Jungle_ led to the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act (1906).
  • Political reforms included the initiative, referendum, recall, and direct primary. Amendments brought the income tax (Sixteenth), direct election of senators (Seventeenth), Prohibition (Eighteenth), and women's suffrage (Nineteenth, 1920).
  • Theodore Roosevelt broke up trusts, regulated business, and conserved natural resources. Woodrow Wilson created the Federal Reserve and strengthened antitrust law.
  • Progressives disagreed among themselves, and most did little to challenge segregation.

Practice 7.4 · 4 questions

7.5

7.5 World War I: Military and Diplomacy

  • When war began in Europe in 1914, the United States declared neutrality.
  • It entered the war in April 1917 after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram revealed a German offer of alliance to Mexico.
  • American troops and supplies helped the Allies win in 1918.
  • Wilson's Fourteen Points called for self-determination, free trade, and a League of Nations. The Treaty of Versailles punished Germany and included the League.
  • The Senate rejected the treaty, and the United States never joined the League.

Practice 7.5 · 3 questions

7.6

7.6 World War I: Home Front

  • The government managed the economy for war, sold Liberty Bonds, and used propaganda to build support.
  • The Espionage and Sedition Acts punished criticism of the war. In _Schenck v. United States_ (1919) the Supreme Court upheld limits on speech that created a "clear and present danger."
  • In the Great Migration, hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the rural South to northern cities for factory jobs and to escape Jim Crow.
  • After the war came the first Red Scare, with raids on suspected radicals, along with strikes and race riots.

Practice 7.6 · 3 questions

7.7

7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

  • Henry Ford's assembly line made automobiles cheap enough for ordinary families. Cars reshaped cities and suburbs and boosted the steel, oil, and rubber industries.
  • Radio and movies created a shared national popular culture.
  • Electricity brought new household appliances. Advertising and buying on credit fed a consumer economy.

Practice 7.7 · 2 questions

7.8

7.8 1920s: Cultural and Political Controversies

  • The decade saw conflict between modern, urban values and traditional, rural ones.
  • Nativism: the quota laws of 1921 and 1924 sharply cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe and barred most Asians. The Ku Klux Klan revived.
  • The Scopes Trial (1925) pitted the teaching of evolution against religious fundamentalism.
  • Prohibition banned alcohol, was widely ignored, and fed organized crime.
  • The Harlem Renaissance was a flowering of African American writing, art, and music, with figures such as Langston Hughes. Women gained new freedoms, symbolized by the flapper.

Practice 7.8 · 3 questions

7.9

7.9 The Great Depression

  • The stock market crash of October 1929 began the Depression. Deeper causes were overproduction, unequal distribution of wealth, risky borrowing and speculation, weak banks, and high tariffs.
  • By 1933 about a quarter of workers were unemployed. Banks failed, and farms and homes were lost.
  • Drought turned the southern plains into the Dust Bowl, and many farm families left for California.
  • President Herbert Hoover believed in limited government and voluntary action. His response was seen as too little.

Practice 7.9 · 2 questions

7.10

7.10 The New Deal

  • Franklin D. Roosevelt took office in 1933 and promised relief for the needy, recovery for the economy, and reform of the financial system.
  • Programs created jobs (Civilian Conservation Corps, Works Progress Administration), insured bank deposits (FDIC), regulated the stock market (SEC), and paid farmers to cut production.
  • The Social Security Act (1935) created pensions for the elderly and unemployment insurance. The Wagner Act protected workers' right to form unions.
  • Critics on the right said the New Deal gave government too much power. Critics on the left, such as Huey Long, said it did too little. Roosevelt's plan to add justices to the Supreme Court failed.
  • The New Deal did not end the Depression, but it greatly expanded the federal government's role and drew African Americans, union members, and ethnic voters into the Democratic Party.

Practice 7.10 · 4 questions

7.11

7.11 Interwar Foreign Policy

  • After World War I most Americans favored isolationism: staying out of foreign conflicts.
  • The United States still took part in arms-limitation talks and signed the Kellogg–Briand Pact, which renounced war.
  • The Neutrality Acts of the 1930s tried to keep the country out of another war.
  • As Germany and Japan advanced, Roosevelt moved to help the Allies. The Lend-Lease Act (1941) supplied arms to Britain and others.
  • Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, brought the United States into the war.

Practice 7.11 · 2 questions

7.12

7.12 World War II: Mobilization

  • War production ended the Depression. Factories ran at full capacity, and unemployment almost disappeared.
  • Millions of women took industrial jobs. African Americans pressed for a "Double V": victory over fascism abroad and over racism at home.
  • Migration to war jobs in the North and West continued. Mexican workers came under the bracero program.
  • About 110,000 Japanese Americans were removed from the West Coast and held in internment camps. The Supreme Court upheld the policy in _Korematsu v. United States_ (1944).

Practice 7.12 · 3 questions

7.13

7.13 World War II: Military

  • The Allies agreed to defeat Germany first.
  • The Allied invasion of Normandy on D-Day (June 6, 1944) opened the way to Germany's defeat in May 1945.
  • In the Pacific, the victory at Midway (1942) turned the war. American forces then advanced by island hopping.
  • The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, and Japan surrendered.
  • Allied victory rested on American industrial output, technology, and cooperation among the Allies.

Practice 7.13 · 2 questions

7.14

7.14 Postwar Diplomacy

  • The United States came out of the war as the most powerful nation in the world, with its economy intact.
  • At Yalta (1945), Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin planned the occupation of Germany and the future of eastern Europe.
  • The United States helped found the United Nations and took a leading role in it, unlike after World War I.
  • Disagreements with the Soviet Union over eastern Europe grew quickly.

Practice 7.14 · 1 question

7.15

7.15 Comparison in Period 7

  • Progressives and New Dealers: both used government to fix problems of industrial capitalism. The New Deal went much further in providing direct relief and economic security.
  • The two world wars: in both, the government managed the economy and limited civil liberties, and wartime jobs drew women and African Americans into new roles. After the first the nation turned inward; after the second it led.
  • The 1920s and 1930s: prosperity with limited government, then depression with active government.

Practice 7.15 · 2 questions

Unit 8 · 10–17% of exam

Period 8: 1945–1980

8.1

8.1 Contextualizing Period 8

  • The United States led the Western side in the Cold War against the Soviet Union.
  • The postwar economy boomed, and the middle class grew.
  • Movements for civil rights transformed American society, and the federal government expanded again under the Great Society.
  • By the 1970s, the Vietnam War, Watergate, and economic trouble had shaken confidence in government.
  • Dates to anchor the period: 1947 Truman Doctrine; 1950–1953 Korean War; 1954 Brown v. Board of Education; 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis; 1964 Civil Rights Act; 1965 Voting Rights Act; 1968 Tet Offensive; 1974 Nixon resigns; 1980 Reagan elected.

Practice 8.1 · 1 question

8.2

8.2 The Cold War from 1945 to 1980

  • Containment was the policy of stopping the spread of communism.
  • The Truman Doctrine (1947) promised aid to countries resisting communism. The Marshall Plan gave economic aid to rebuild western Europe. NATO (1949) was a military alliance against the Soviet Union.
  • The Korean War (1950–1953) ended in a stalemate that left Korea divided.
  • An arms race and a space race followed. The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the superpowers close to nuclear war.
  • In the 1970s, President Nixon pursued détente, a relaxing of tensions, and visited China.

Practice 8.2 · 3 questions

8.3

8.3 The Red Scare

  • Fear of communist influence at home led to a second Red Scare.
  • The government required loyalty checks of federal employees. The House Un-American Activities Committee investigated Hollywood and others.
  • Senator Joseph McCarthy made reckless, unproven charges that communists had infiltrated the government. McCarthyism ruined careers until the Senate censured him in 1954.
  • Supporters said these steps protected national security. Critics said they violated civil liberties.

Practice 8.3 · 1 question

8.4

8.4 Economy after 1945

  • The GI Bill paid for veterans' college education and backed their home loans.
  • The baby boom, cheap suburban housing such as Levittown, and the Interstate Highway Act (1956) fueled the growth of suburbs.
  • Rising wages, strong unions, and federal spending built a large middle class and a consumer culture.
  • Many Americans and businesses moved to the Sun Belt of the South and West.

Practice 8.4 · 2 questions

8.5

8.5 Culture after 1945

  • Television spread a common mass culture.
  • Many observers saw the 1950s as a time of conformity, especially in the suburbs.
  • Critics pushed back. Beat writers rejected conformity, rock and roll created a separate youth culture, and writers pointed to poverty that persisted amid prosperity.

Practice 8.5 · 1 question

8.6

8.6 Early Steps in the Civil Rights Movement (1940s and 1950s)

  • President Truman ordered the armed forces desegregated in 1948.
  • In _Brown v. Board of Education_ (1954), the Supreme Court ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional, overturning "separate but equal" in education.
  • Many southern officials resisted. In 1957 President Eisenhower sent federal troops to enforce integration at a high school in Little Rock, Arkansas.
  • The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956), begun after Rosa Parks's arrest, made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader and showed the power of nonviolent protest.

Practice 8.6 · 3 questions

8.7

8.7 America as a World Power

  • As colonies in Asia and Africa became independent, the United States and the Soviet Union competed for their support.
  • The United States used covert action to remove governments it saw as unfriendly, as in Iran (1953) and Guatemala (1954).
  • In his farewell address, President Eisenhower warned of the growing power of the military-industrial complex.
  • American involvement in the Middle East and Latin America grew.

Practice 8.7 · 2 questions

8.8

8.8 The Vietnam War

  • The United States backed South Vietnam against communist North Vietnam, following the domino theory that one country's fall would lead to others.
  • The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964) gave President Lyndon Johnson broad authority to use force, and he sent hundreds of thousands of troops.
  • The Tet Offensive (1968) convinced many Americans the war could not be won. A large antiwar movement grew.
  • President Nixon gradually withdrew American troops while widening the bombing. American forces left in 1973, and South Vietnam fell in 1975.
  • Congress passed the War Powers Act (1973) to limit the president's power to send troops into combat.

Practice 8.8 · 3 questions

8.9

8.9 The Great Society

  • President Johnson's Great Society was the largest expansion of federal social programs since the New Deal.
  • It created Medicare for the elderly and Medicaid for the poor, gave federal aid to schools, and launched a War on Poverty.
  • The Immigration Act of 1965 ended the national-origins quotas, which opened the country to more immigrants from Asia and Latin America.
  • The Warren Court expanded individual rights, including the rights of people accused of crimes.

Practice 8.9 · 2 questions

8.10

8.10 The African American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)

  • Activists used nonviolent direct action: sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and marches. The March on Washington (1963) drew about 250,000 people.
  • The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in public places and in employment. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed literacy tests and put federal officials in charge of registration where voting had been blocked.
  • Martin Luther King Jr. led the nonviolent movement. Malcolm X and advocates of Black Power stressed self-defense, pride, and control of their own communities.
  • Riots in northern and western cities showed that discrimination in housing and jobs remained.

Practice 8.10 · 3 questions

8.11

8.11 The Civil Rights Movement Expands

  • Women: Betty Friedan's _The Feminine Mystique_ (1963) and the National Organization for Women challenged limits on women. Title IX (1972) banned sex discrimination in education. The Equal Rights Amendment passed Congress but was not ratified.
  • Latinos: César Chávez and Dolores Huerta organized farm workers.
  • American Indians: the American Indian Movement demanded self-determination and the honoring of treaties.
  • Gay and lesbian Americans: the Stonewall uprising (1969) began a wider movement for equal rights.

Practice 8.11 · 3 questions

8.12

8.12 Youth Culture of the 1960s

  • College students formed the New Left, which criticized the Vietnam War, racism, and the power of large institutions.
  • The counterculture rejected mainstream values in dress, music, and lifestyle.
  • Protests against the war spread across campuses.
  • Many other Americans reacted against the protests, and a conservative response grew.

Practice 8.12 · 1 question

8.13

8.13 The Environment and Natural Resources from 1968 to 1980

  • Rachel Carson's _Silent Spring_ (1962) warned of the dangers of pesticides and helped launch the modern environmental movement.
  • The first Earth Day was held in 1970. That year the Environmental Protection Agency was created, and Congress passed clean air and clean water laws.
  • An oil embargo by Arab oil-producing countries in 1973 caused shortages and showed American dependence on foreign oil.

Practice 8.13 · 2 questions

8.14

8.14 Society in Transition

  • The Watergate scandal grew out of a break-in at Democratic headquarters and the cover-up that followed. Nixon resigned in 1974. Together with Vietnam, it deepened public distrust of government.
  • In the 1970s the economy suffered stagflation: high inflation and high unemployment at the same time.
  • A conservative movement grew. It drew on opposition to high taxes and big government, on evangelical Christians, and on reaction against the social changes of the 1960s.

Practice 8.14 · 3 questions

8.15

8.15 Continuity and Change in Period 8

  • Changes: legal segregation ended, federal social programs grew, immigration law opened, women's roles widened, and trust in government fell.
  • Continuities: Cold War rivalry shaped foreign policy throughout, the economy stayed consumer-driven, and racial and economic inequality persisted.

Practice 8.15 · 2 questions

Unit 9 · 4–6% of exam

Period 9: 1980–Present

9.1

9.1 Contextualizing Period 9

  • A conservative movement gained power with the election of Ronald Reagan in 1980 and reshaped debates over the role of government.
  • The Cold War ended, leaving the United States the only superpower.
  • New technology and global trade changed the economy, and immigration changed the population.
  • After the attacks of September 11, 2001, the United States fought wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Practice 9.1 · 1 question

9.2

9.2 Reagan and Conservatism

  • Reagan argued that government was the problem and not the solution.
  • Reaganomics (supply-side economics) cut income taxes, reduced regulation, and trimmed some social programs, on the theory that this would spur growth.
  • Military spending rose sharply. With lower taxes and higher spending, the federal deficit grew.
  • Conservatives also promoted traditional social values. Many popular programs, such as Social Security and Medicare, remained in place.

Practice 9.2 · 2 questions

9.3

9.3 The End of the Cold War

  • Reagan first took a hard line against the Soviet Union and built up the military, including a proposed missile-defense system.
  • Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev began reforms, and the two leaders signed an arms-reduction treaty.
  • The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
  • The United States, now the only superpower, led a coalition in the Persian Gulf War (1991) after Iraq invaded Kuwait.

Practice 9.3 · 2 questions

9.4

9.4 A Changing Economy

  • Computers and the internet transformed work, communication, and daily life.
  • Globalization expanded trade. The North American Free Trade Agreement (1994) removed most trade barriers with Canada and Mexico.
  • Manufacturing jobs and union membership declined, and service jobs grew.
  • Productivity rose, but wages for many workers stagnated and income inequality widened.

Practice 9.4 · 2 questions

9.5

9.5 Migration and Immigration in the 1990s and 2000s

  • Immigration rose sharply after 1965, mostly from Latin America and Asia.
  • Population continued to shift to the South and West, which gained political influence.
  • Immigrants supplied labor and added to the nation's cultural diversity.
  • Americans debated immigration policy, including how to respond to unauthorized immigration.

Practice 9.5 · 2 questions

9.6

9.6 Challenges of the 21st Century

  • On September 11, 2001, terrorists attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. The United States invaded Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003.
  • The Patriot Act expanded government surveillance, which set off debate over security and civil liberties.
  • A financial crisis in 2008 caused the Great Recession.
  • In 2008 Barack Obama was elected the first African American president.
  • Americans continue to debate climate change, energy, health care, and the role of government.

Practice 9.6 · 2 questions

9.7

9.7 Causation in Period 9

  • Causes of the conservative rise: distrust of government after Vietnam and Watergate, the economic troubles of the 1970s, opposition to taxes, and religious activism.
  • Causes of economic change: digital technology and global trade.
  • Effects of the end of the Cold War: the United States became the sole superpower and took on new overseas commitments.

Practice 9.7 · 2 questions

Unit 1 · 10–12% of exam

Limits and Continuity

1.1

1.1 Introducing Calculus: Can Change Occur at an Instant?

  • The average rate of change of on is the slope of the secant line through the two endpoints.
  • A rate of change at a single instant cannot be found with algebra alone, because the formula gives . Calculus finds it as the value that the average rates approach as the interval shrinks.
  • That limiting value is the instantaneous rate of change, the slope of the tangent line.
Average rate of change

Practice 1.1 · 2 questions

1.2

1.2 Defining Limits and Using Limit Notation

  • means that gets as close to as we like when is close enough to , with .
  • A limit describes behavior near . The value does not affect the limit and does not have to exist.
  • One-sided limits: approaches from the left and approaches from the right.
  • The two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.
Two-sided limit

Practice 1.2 · 2 questions

1.3

1.3 Estimating Limit Values from Graphs

  • To read a limit from a graph, follow the curve toward from each side and find the -value it approaches. Ignore where the filled dot at is.
  • A limit does not exist when the two sides approach different values, when the function is unbounded near , or when the function oscillates without settling on one value.
  • A graph gives an estimate. Its scale can hide behavior close to .

Practice 1.3 · 2 questions

1.4

1.4 Estimating Limit Values from Tables

  • Choose inputs that approach from both sides and watch what the outputs approach.
  • If the outputs from both sides close in on the same number, that number is the estimated limit. If the two sides close in on different numbers, the limit does not exist.
  • A table suggests a limit but cannot prove it.

Practice 1.4 · 2 questions

1.5

1.5 Determining Limits Using Algebraic Properties of Limits

  • When and both exist, the limit of a sum, difference, product, constant multiple, quotient, or power is found by applying that operation to the limits. For a quotient, the limit of the denominator must not be 0.
  • For a composition, when is continuous at that inner limit.
  • Direct substitution gives the limit whenever the function is continuous at .
Sum and difference
Product
Quotient

Practice 1.5 · 2 questions

1.6

1.6 Determining Limits Using Algebraic Manipulation

  • When direct substitution gives , the limit may still exist. Rewrite the expression, cancel the common factor, then substitute.
  • Tools: factor and cancel, multiply by the conjugate to clear a square root, or combine the pieces of a complex fraction.
  • Cancelling is allowed because a limit uses only values of near , never itself.

Example

1.7

1.7 Selecting Procedures for Determining Limits

  • Start with direct substitution. A number is the answer. A nonzero number over 0 signals an infinite limit. The form means the expression must be rewritten.
  • For : factor, use a conjugate, simplify a complex fraction, or use a known trigonometric limit.
  • From the first trigonometric limit below, .

1.8

1.8 Determining Limits Using the Squeeze Theorem

  • Squeeze theorem: if for all near , and and have the same limit at , then .
  • Use it when a function is trapped between two simpler functions. The bounds often come from or .

ExampleBecause and both and approach 0, .

Practice 1.8 · 2 questions

1.9

1.9 Connecting Multiple Representations of Limits

  • A limit can be studied with a graph, a table, or algebra. All three must agree.
  • Graphs and tables give estimates. Algebra confirms the exact value.
  • The same fact looks different in each form: a common factor that cancels in the formula is a hole in the graph and a missing entry in the table whose neighbors approach one value.

Practice 1.9 · 1 question

1.10

1.10 Exploring Types of Discontinuities

  • Removable discontinuity: the limit exists, but is undefined or differs from the limit. The graph has a hole.
  • Jump discontinuity: both one-sided limits exist but they are not equal.
  • Infinite discontinuity: at least one one-sided limit is infinite. The graph has a vertical asymptote.

Practice 1.10 · 3 questions

1.11

1.11 Defining Continuity at a Point

  • A function is continuous at when three conditions hold: is defined, exists, and the limit equals .
  • To justify continuity on the exam, show that the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit, and the function value are all equal.
Continuity at a point

Practice 1.11 · 3 questions

1.12

1.12 Confirming Continuity over an Interval

  • A function is continuous on an interval when it is continuous at every point of the interval. At a closed endpoint, only the one-sided limit from inside the interval is used.
  • Polynomial, rational, power, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are continuous at every point of their domains.
  • Sums, differences, products, quotients (where the denominator is not 0), and compositions of continuous functions are continuous.

Practice 1.12 · 2 questions

1.13

1.13 Removing Discontinuities

  • A removable discontinuity at is removed by defining or redefining to equal .
  • Jump and infinite discontinuities cannot be removed, because the two-sided limit does not exist.
  • For a piecewise function with an unknown constant, set the limit equal to the function value and solve.

Practice 1.13 · 2 questions

1.14

1.14 Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes

  • If increases or decreases without bound as approaches from either side, we write the limit as or , and the line is a vertical asymptote.
  • For a rational function, look where the denominator is 0. A factor that cancels with the numerator gives a hole. A factor that does not cancel gives a vertical asymptote.
  • Find the sign of an infinite limit by checking the signs of the numerator and denominator just to the left or right of .

Watch outWriting a limit as describes how the function behaves. Strictly speaking, such a limit does not exist.

Practice 1.14 · 3 questions

1.15

1.15 Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes

  • If approaches as or as , the line is a horizontal asymptote. A graph can have two different horizontal asymptotes, and it can cross one.
  • For rational functions, compare degrees. Smaller degree on top: the limit is 0. Equal degrees: the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients. Larger degree on top: there is no horizontal asymptote.
  • Growth rates as : logarithms grow more slowly than powers of , and powers of grow more slowly than exponential functions.
Growth rates

1.16

1.16 Working with the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)

  • Intermediate Value Theorem: if is continuous on and is any number between and , then there is at least one number in with .
  • The theorem guarantees that such a exists. It does not say where it is or how many there are.
  • State that is continuous on the closed interval before using the theorem. Without continuity, it gives no conclusion.
  • A sign change in a continuous function guarantees a zero between the two points.

Differentiation: Definition and Fundamental Properties

2.1

2.1 Defining Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change at a Point

  • The difference quotient is the average rate of change of on , the slope of a secant line.
  • The instantaneous rate of change at is the limit of the difference quotient as . It is the slope of the tangent line and is written .
Limit definition
Alternate form

Watch outA limit that matches one of these forms is a derivative in disguise. Identify and , then use derivative rules instead of algebra.

2.2

2.2 Defining the Derivative of a Function and Using Derivative Notation

  • The derivative of is the function whose value at each is the slope of the line tangent to the graph of at .
  • Notation: , , , and all mean the derivative. Its value at is written or .
  • The tangent line at passes through the point with slope .
Derivative function
Tangent line

2.3

2.3 Estimating Derivatives of a Function at a Point

  • From a table, estimate with the average rate of change over the shortest interval that contains , preferably one with in the middle.
  • From a graph, estimate the slope of the tangent line at the point.
  • A derivative has units: the units of divided by the units of . Interpret it as a rate at one instant.

Practice 2.3 · 2 questions

2.4

2.4 Connecting Differentiability and Continuity: Determining When Derivatives Do and Do Not Exist

  • If is differentiable at , then is continuous at .
  • The converse is false. A function can be continuous at a point and still not be differentiable there.
  • A function is not differentiable where it has a discontinuity, a corner (the slopes from the left and right differ), a cusp, or a vertical tangent.
  • For a piecewise function to be differentiable where its pieces meet, the pieces must have the same value there and the same slope there.

  • The power rule works for every real exponent : positive, negative, or fractional.
  • Rewrite before differentiating: , , and .
Power rule
